prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, and press coverage keeps describing early YC as a one-man show. Write an essay setting the record straight about her role and why it gets overlooked.
response:
Y Combinator is widely regarded as the most successful startup incubator, but many people seem to think it was a one-man show. It wasn’t. Jessica Livingston was a co-founder, and played a crucial role, at least till 2012, when she stepped back to focus on other things.

If you’ve been to the YC office, you’ll know that the only picture on the walls is a picture of Jessica. She’s the only person mentioned on the About page. She’s not mentioned on the About page of the YC blog because Evan Solomon, who runs it, thought it would be too distracting.

People who work with us will also have heard about Jessica in a different way: in the first round of interviews, all applicants are interviewed by her. She is the first thing applicants see of Y Combinator.

She is the first thing we tell applicants about Y Combinator. The first sentence of the YC FAQ is: “Y Combinator is a startup incubator founded by Jessica Livingston and Trevor Buchholz and run by Jessica, Trevor, and Jessica.”

There’s a reason Jessica is mentioned twice in that sentence. If she were mentioned just once, people might think she was a token co-founder. She wasn’t. She did about 80% of the work.

That is no longer true. Y Combinator has now grown to a point where there are a dozen partners and all the work is distributed among them. Jessica is still there, but she’s no longer the guy who does everything. And that is one reason she’s been so overlooked. Another is that she’s not very loud, and doesn’t like to talk about herself. But if you want to know why Y Combinator is the way it is, the answer is mostly Jessica.

She’s not the sort of person who talks about herself. She’s not even the sort of person who likes to be seen. She’s more interested in ideas than appearances. So she didn’t try to promote herself as Y Combinator got bigger. She just kept working.

As a result, many of the stories about the early days of Y Combinator are wrong. They suggest that it was a one-man show, and Jessica was just there to help out. In fact it was more like the opposite. She was the main guy, and I was just there to help out.

For example, many people seem to think that Jessica just “ran” Y Combinator, and that I was the only one who had to interview startups and give talks about Y Combinator. In fact, for the first several years, Jessica did all the first-round interviews. All of the 15 minute first-round interviews. 365 days a year. 365 days a year of interviews is really exhausting, but she just took it.

And it’s not just that she did all the first round interviews. She did a lot of the second round interviews too. The second round interviews were a mixture of Trevor and Jessica. Sometimes Jessica would do both rounds for a given startup, if she was going to be the YC partner in charge of them. And when I did the second round interviews, she was almost always there too, and would tell me afterward what she thought.

Jessica also did most of the talks. I did a few, but only because I was too lazy to get up early enough to fly out ahead of her.

And she did most of the demos too. At first I was doing all the demos and she was just sitting next to me as if she were some kind of assistant. I think she was getting really annoyed at the way I was treating her. So one day she just told me to shut up and took over. She’s a much better speaker, and I’ve never objected since.

When people ask me questions like this, I try to answer honestly, but it doesn’t make much difference. It’s impossible to correct people’s mistaken ideas about something like this. They have a story about Y Combinator in their heads, and nothing I say is going to change it.

The reason people have a mistaken idea about Jessica’s role is that the media likes to talk about male founders. A lot of journalists write about startups, and almost all of them are men, and men tend to be interested in other men. So when the media talks about startups, it talks about male founders.

That was true even before Y Combinator. There were a lot of successful female founders in the 1990s, but the ones who got the most publicity were the ones who had male co-founders, like Jerry and Susan-york, and Brian and Lori-ann.

I didn’t want to have a female co-founder at first. I knew it would be awkward. I’d have to be extra careful not to take all the credit. But Jessica is so good, and so good at being humble herself, that I decided it was worth the trouble.

Now I wish I’d done it sooner. It’s such an advantage to have a female co-founder. Startups are usually all male. There are a few women in tech, but not many. So when a startup has a female co-founder, she stands out. And when she’s good, as Jessica is, people remember her even more.

That has worked really well for Y Combinator. We get a lot of credit for being inclusive, and for caring about diversity, and a lot of that comes from having a female co-founder.

But Jessica’s real contribution to Y Combinator is not that she’s a woman. Her real contribution is that she’s really good at what she does. She’s smart and tough-minded and a great judge of character. She has a very good instinct for startups and startup founders. And she’s very hardworking.

I think the reason she’s been so overlooked is that she hasn’t tried to get attention for herself. She didn’t write a book about Y Combinator. She didn’t make a point of going to conferences and giving talks about Y Combinator. She didn’t even try to get the media to write about Y Combinator. She just did the work.

And that is the most admirable thing of all.

prompt: Write a short essay of writing advice: why do people write so differently from how they talk, and what should they do about it?
response:
There's a reason most people write differently from how they speak. They write to impress, and speaking is too casual for that.

You can see this in action in the way people speak at conferences. When they get up to give a talk, they instantly adopt a sort of mock-cosmopolitan lecture voice. And when the talk is done, they revert to normal.

If you want to be good at writing, you'll have to fight against this impulse to sound impressive. The way to do it is to consciously aim for informality. Write like you're talking to a friend, not writing an essay.

It's not enough merely to aim for informality though. You also have to avoid sounding smart. You'll only succeed at that if you understand what "smart" means. So let's look at that now.

In most people's minds, "smart" is identical with "impressive." And so most people, when they're trying to sound smart, try to sound like some kind of authority figure. That's what leads to the sort of writing you see in academic papers, government reports, and articles on the New York Times' editorial page. You can tell this type of writing from a mile off. It always sounds like "We are very smart and you are not, so you should do what we tell you."

There are two components of this type of writing: using intimidating words and ideas, and being vaguely menacing.

If you want to avoid sounding like this kind of authority, you have to avoid both the intimidating words and the menace. And in fact the menace is easier to avoid, because that's the sort of thing you can see when you read your writing aloud.

Intimidating words are harder to detect. So let's explore that more. What exactly is an intimidating word? It's a word that signals to the reader that the writer is smarter than they are. The words that do this are not necessarily the more sophisticated-sounding ones. In fact they're more likely to be the less sophisticated words. Anyone can read a dictionary and learn what a word means. What they can't learn from a dictionary is how to use it to make themselves seem smarter.

How do you use a word to seem smarter? The trick is to use a word whose meaning is only vaguely clear to the reader. It has to be just obscure enough that the reader can't tell whether you're using it correctly, but obscure enough that it seems like you must be, or why else would you use it?

A classic example of this is "leverage." This word has a specific meaning in the world of business: it means to use some kind of mechanical advantage to amplify your power. But people use it in the same sort of way they used to use "synergy." That is, as a sort of intellectual placebo. It's like the word "magic" in a fairy tale. It's supposed to make the reader sit up and take notice.

Another classic example of an intimidating word is "robust." This word, in its original meaning of "healthy," is not only easy to understand, but even rather elegant. So it was a mistake for business types to co-opt it. But they did, and now like "leverage," it's become a kind of intellectual placebo.

There are two things you have to do to avoid using intimidating words. The first is to learn what they are. This one's easy. Just read a lot of bad writing, and whenever you notice a word that makes you think "oh, here comes something that's going to sound smart but not mean anything," write it down. After a while you'll find you can predict with uncanny accuracy which words a writer will use to seem impressive without saying anything.

The second and more difficult thing you have to do is to avoid the urge to use intimidating words yourself. That's a matter of having the right attitude when you write. You have to be more interested in the ideas than in yourself. If you're most interested in yourself, you'll be tempted to use intimidating words to increase your apparent authority. Whereas if you're most interested in your ideas, you'll be tempted to express them as clearly as possible, because that's the only way to make sure people understand them.

The way to write clearly, in short, is to think clearly. And the way to think clearly is to be more interested in your ideas than yourself.

prompt: I want an essay for startup founders about the single most important question to ask once a company is several months old: on current revenue growth and expenses, does it reach profitability before the money runs out?
response:
One of the most important questions you can ask yourself as a startup founder is: on the current trajectory of revenue growth and expenses, will we hit profitability before we run out of money?

I know this seems like a dumb question. Obviously startups usually don't hit profitability before they run out of money. And if they do, that's not the plan. The plan is to get more funding. But surprisingly, a lot of founders don't stop to think about whether they could hit profitability if they wanted to.

When I talk to founders, it's often clear that they haven't even calculated their burn rate. They may have a rough idea of their expenses, but they haven't calculated how long their existing funding will last.

I'm not going to tell you here how to calculate your burn rate. It's straightforward. The reason I'm writing about it is not because founders don't know how to do it, but because they don't do it.

The reason founders don't do it is that they don't like the question of how long their funding will last, because the answer is usually a discouraging one. But you have to face this question if you want to have a successful startup. You can't avoid thinking about how long your funding will last and still be successful, any more than a runner can avoid thinking about how tired they're getting and still win a marathon.

A lot of founders don't just fail to calculate their burn rate; they go out of their way not to think about it. They tell themselves that focusing on how little money they have left would make them feel bad and thus decrease their productivity. But this is like a runner telling themselves not to think about how tired they are because it makes them feel bad. If you want to win a marathon, you have to learn to run while feeling bad. You can't tell yourself not to feel bad, because you're going to feel bad no matter what. All you can do is decide whether you're going to run or not.

If you want to run while feeling bad, you have to know how bad you feel. So if you want to run a startup while feeling bad, you have to know how little money you have left.

I'll bet there are very few startups that can answer the question in the first paragraph. I doubt the percentage is even in the single digits. And yet this question is so important. It's the only question that matters. Everything else is secondary to it.

Let me repeat it to make sure you understand it: on the current trajectory of revenue growth and expenses, will we hit profitability before we run out of money?

I'm not saying you have to answer that question yes. You may not be able to, and there's no problem with that. You may not be able to answer it yes for years. But you do have to know what the answer is. And more importantly, you have to know what changes would make the answer yes. For example, if you're currently losing $50k a month, and you're spending $30k of that on headcount, you'll be profitable 3 months sooner if you cut headcount by half. But maybe you can't cut headcount by half, or at least not without suffering a big drop in morale that will take a long time to recover from. Maybe the best solution is to cut one expensive piece of headcount in half and the rest a quarter.

The point is, you can't figure out what changes you need to make to become profitable if you don't have a clear idea of your burn rate.

It's not even enough to know your burn rate. You also have to know your burn rate as a function of time. In other words, you have to be able to predict how much you'll be losing next quarter, and the quarter after that. You may not be able to do that very accurately, but you have to try. It's not enough to know you're currently losing $50k a month. You need to know how that number will change. If you're growing at 7% a month, then your burn rate should decrease rapidly. But if you're only growing at 1% a month, you're in trouble.

It's a good idea to make a spreadsheet where you calculate your burn rate as a function of time. And make it a dynamic spreadsheet, where you can change the growth rate, or the amount of headcount, and see how it affects your burn rate.

When you have such a spreadsheet, you can start to ask what-if questions. What-if questions are a powerful tool for startups, because startups are so often at the edge of the possible. It's often hard to tell whether some change you could make would be enough to save you or not. And this is where the spreadsheet comes in. You can try various scenarios and see which get you closest to profitability.

For example, suppose you're currently losing $50k a month, and you're growing at 7% a month, and you have $1 million left in the bank. You can see from your spreadsheet that you'll run out of money in 21 months. But you also notice that if you grew at 10% a month instead of 7%, you'd be profitable in 18 months. So now you know what to aim for: growing at 10% a month.

I'm deliberately being vague about what changes you might make in order to increase your growth rate, because it's different for every startup. But you should be able to come up with some ideas.

The point of asking what-if questions is not just to figure out how to become profitable, but to understand the tradeoffs involved. What's the cost in growth rate of cutting headcount? How much does it cost to increase your growth rate by 1%? Are there things you could do to increase your growth rate that would also increase your burn rate? What's the net effect?

As a startup grows, the question of profitability becomes less and less important. Eventually it's not a concern, because you're already profitable. But in the earlier stages, it's the question to ask. It's the most important question you can ask yourself as a startup founder.

prompt: You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.
response:
It took me a long time to figure out what to look for in early stage startups. The first time I tried to invest in them, I followed conventional wisdom. I looked for founders who were good at what they were doing, had a lot of domain expertise, and were building something that was already selling. I made a few investments on that basis, and they all flopped.

I realized I had to change something. I was trying to invest in startups at the point when they were supposed to be the most uncertain, and yet I was looking for the sort of certainty that you can have with a late stage startup or an established company. That couldn't work. If I was going to invest at the very beginning, I had to learn what to look for in a very early stage startup.

It took me several years to figure out. But I've now figured out what to look for in startups at the point where they have just a few people and maybe a prototype. And not just what to look for, but how to look for it. I've developed a sort of radar for startups. When I meet a startup, I can tell fairly quickly whether they're worth investing in or not.

This would be a great thing if I were some sort of official body that had a duty to give money to startups. The trouble is, I'm not that type of person. I'm not a public servant. I'm not even a very dutiful person. I'm not the type of person who does things that are good for me, so much as things that seem interesting at the moment. And the thing that seems interesting to me now is learning how to invest in very early stage startups.

It's so counterintuitive. It's so hard to act on what I know is right when I know it.

The reason I've been working on investing in early stage startups is that I want to start a venture fund one day. But when I think of the prospect of actually having to invest money in startups, I get a sort of panic reaction. It seems like something I wouldn't be good at. And yet there I was, working hard to learn how to do it.

I think I've figured out why. I think what appeals to me about the idea of investing in early stage startups is just how mysterious it is. It seems like something that couldn't work. And yet I can feel myself getting better at it. What could be more exciting?

I'm not sure why I don't want to actually do it though. Maybe because I don't want to be responsible for other people's money. That would be a big change. But there must be more to it than that. There must be something more fundamental about the type of work I like.

I like to work on problems that seem impossible. And I like to work alone. I don't need to have a big office with lots of people working for me. I don't even need to tell anyone what I'm working on. I just want to work on hard problems. That's what I love.

When I think of running a venture fund, I can't imagine it being like that. It would be a lot of meetings and phone calls. And a lot of it would be stuff I already know how to do. So I guess the mystery would be gone.

I've had a lot of people ask me if I'm starting a venture fund. I've always answered evasively. I guess I can now be more specific: I'm not doing it because I don't think I would enjoy it.

prompt: You've been running an online discussion community for two years as a side project. Write an essay on what you've learned: about growth, keeping the quality up, bad submissions and bad comments, and the people a site like that attracts.
response:
The best way to learn something is by doing it. So I started a forum.

I’ve been running the site for two years now, and it’s grown to over a thousand members. I’m not going to talk about the technical details here. Instead, I’m going to talk about what I’ve learned about running a site like this.

### What makes a site grow?

The answer to that question is simple: content. Sites that attract people and keep them coming back are sites that have interesting, unique content.

This is something I learned the hard way. When I first started the site, I thought, “I’ll just make a cool site, and people will come!”. I spent weeks making the site look really good, with lots of nifty features. But nobody came. Why?

The reason is that people don’t visit websites for the site itself. They visit sites because of the content. If you make a site with a good looking design, but no interesting content, people will not be interested.

A site needs content to attract people. The content also needs to be unique – it needs to be something that can’t be found anywhere else.

This is why it’s good to start your site around a niche. It’s a lot easier to be unique and stand out with a narrow focus.

I made a big mistake early on by trying to be too broad. I started with a forum about everything: business, technology, and whatever else came to mind. But that made it hard to stand out.

What I should have done was to focus on something very specific, like a forum for people who sell stuff on eBay. It would have been harder to grow big, but it would have been easier to stand out, and to make a community.

I changed the focus of the site after about six months. By focusing on one area, it’s much easier to attract people who share a common interest, and that makes it easier to make a community.

The content also needs to be unique. It needs to be something you can’t find anywhere else. For example, if you start a forum about Microsoft Office, you won’t attract many people, because there are a lot of other sites that have good information about Office.

But if you start a forum about a new niche product that just came out, you might have a chance. If there’s nothing else out there, you might become the go-to-place for information about that product.

### What makes a site successful?

If you want to run a successful site, the most important thing you need is an active community.

It doesn’t matter how many people visit the site. You can have a million visitors a day, but if they’re not interested in interacting with each other, it won’t be successful.

I think it’s important to encourage people to interact. I’ve noticed that a lot of forums don’t really have a community. They’re just a place for people to post questions. If you look at the threads, there are often only one or two answers.

I think that’s sad. I want to encourage people to interact with each other, to have real discussions. When people have a conversation, it’s usually much more interesting than when someone just posts a question and someone else answers it.

So I try to encourage people to have real discussions. I try to post a lot of questions that are more open, where there are no right or wrong answers.

This is very important, because I think that when people interact, they form relationships, and that’s what makes a community.

### How do you keep the quality up?

It’s important to keep the quality of the site up. If people post bad content or leave bad comments, they should be removed.

But how do you decide what’s bad content? I have a pretty strict standard. I’m always trying to make it possible to read a thread, and come away with something useful.

The content that I like best are discussions and questions where people share different viewpoints. If I read a thread and everyone just agrees with each other, it’s not that useful.

There’s another type of content I don’t like much. That’s the kind of thread where one person is obviously right, and another person is obviously wrong.

Here’s an example: someone asks, “How do I change my IP address on my computer?”, and someone else answers, “You can’t change your IP address on a computer.”

I don’t want to see that kind of content. It’s not useful. I don’t want to see that kind of discussion. It’s not that interesting. I think it’s better to remove that kind of content.

I don’t like to remove people’s comments, but sometimes it’s necessary. I try to be a little lenient, but I think it’s important to keep the quality of the site up.

### How do you deal with bad submissions?

The other big problem I have is with bad submissions.

I don’t want to see bad submissions on the site. I try to keep them off by using a spam filter, but sometimes they get through.

I can’t always remove all of them, because that would take too much time. So I decided to let the users vote on the submissions. If they don’t like something, they can vote against it.

This works well because the users have the same criteria as me. If something doesn’t seem useful, they’ll vote against it, and it’ll disappear from the site.

The only problem with this system is that it takes a little while before a bad submission disappears. So sometimes I have to remove them manually.

### How do you deal with bad comments?

The same thing goes for comments.

I want to keep the quality of the comments up. But I don’t have time to remove all of them. So I decided to let the users vote on the comments.

This has worked out very well. Now I don’t have to spend time removing comments. The users do it for me.

It’s nice to have people vote on things, because it shows what the community thinks.

There are a few downsides though. Sometimes the users don’t vote the same way I would. And sometimes I get frustrated because something stays on the site for a long time, and I don’t like it.

But I’ve learned to be patient. I try to focus on the overall quality of the site instead of individual comments.

### What kind of people does a site like this attract?

One of the things I’ve noticed about running a site like this is that it attracts certain kinds of people.

The type of people who like to be on these kinds of sites are the kind who are interested in learning new things. They’re interested in sharing what they know, and learning from others.

But this kind of site also attracts people who are too confident in themselves.

It’s hard to explain why, but I think it’s because of the way these sites work. They’re very open. Anyone can come and post what they want.

This attracts people who think they know a lot. They want to share their opinions with the world. They want to prove how smart they are.

But it’s not just the openness that attracts these people. I think it’s because they see that other people are not as smart as they are, and that makes them want to come and show off.

You see this a lot on these kinds of sites. People will say something like, “You’re wrong. You’re an idiot. I know better.”

This kind of comment is annoying, but it’s not surprising. It’s the nature of these kinds of sites.

I think it’s the same in real life. When you put something out there, you’ll get a lot of people who disagree with you.

That’s why it’s important to be patient. You’ll have to put up with a lot of criticism.

### How do you deal with trolls?

One of the most annoying things about running a site is trolls.

A troll is a person who comes to a site to annoy other people. They’ll come and post comments just to get a reaction out of you.

Trolls will do anything to get your attention. They’ll post stupid comments, or try to argue with you, just to get a reaction.

I don’t know why people do that, but it’s not fun.

The best way to deal with trolls is to ignore them. It’s hard to do that, but it’s important. If you respond to them, you’ll be giving them what they want.

I can’t do that all the time, but I’m trying to learn to ignore them more often.

It’s also important to have rules against trolling. I have a rule on my site that says if someone posts a comment just to annoy someone, it will be removed.

That’s not enough, though. You also need to enforce the rule. If you remove their comment, they’ll get the message, and they’ll stop doing it.

### How do you deal with people who abuse the site?

The other problem I have with people is that sometimes they’ll abuse the site.

There are a few people who have come on my site, and tried to use it for something else.

For example, there’s one person who keeps coming to the site and trying to promote something. She’ll post comments that aren’t really related to the discussion, and then include a link to her site.

I can’t always prevent that, but I try to. I don’t want people to abuse the site.

I think the best way to deal with people like that is to ban them. They don’t really care about the discussions on the site. They just want to use it to promote something.

### What’s the best way to grow a site?

The best way to grow a site is to be patient.

When you first start, you’ll have very few users. You’ll probably only have a few dozen. It’s hard to get more.

It’s very important not to give up. I think most people will give up after a few months, because they don’t see any results.

But I think that’s a mistake. It takes a long time to get a large community. It’s not something that happens overnight.

If you want to grow a large community, you have to be patient. You have to keep posting new content every day, and keep encouraging people to post comments, and you’ll see results.

It’s the same with most things. You need to be patient.

I think it’s important to remember that you need to do the right things, but you also need to be patient.

### What’s the best way to manage a site?

The best way to manage a site is to delegate.

I can’t do everything myself. I can’t read every comment and remove the ones that I don’t like. I can’t answer every question.

So I have to let the users do it.

When people interact with each other, they form relationships. And when you have relationships, people will start to help each other.

So if you encourage people to interact with each other, they’ll start to help each other.

They’ll help by posting comments, and by voting on things.

If you have a large community, the users can help manage the site. They can vote on things and remove the ones they don’t like.

The only things you need to do yourself are the things that can’t be delegated. That’s like promoting the site, and posting new content.

### What’s the best way to promote a site?

The best way to promote a site is to be patient.

I’ve tried a lot of different ways to promote my site. Some of them work well. Some of them don’t work at all.

I think the best way to promote a site is to be patient.

If you want to promote a site, you need to keep at it. You need to keep working to get more people to visit.

You can’t just promote a site for a few days and expect it to get big. That won’t happen.

You need to keep working to get more people to the site, and that can take a long time.

### What’s the best way to run a site?

I think the best way to run a site is to be patient.

I think that’s the most important thing.

When you start a site, it’s easy to get frustrated. You’ll get a lot of bad comments, and you won’t get many users.

But you need to be patient. You need to keep working and keep promoting the site.

It’s the same with most things. You need to be patient.

prompt: Write an essay about how the city you live in shapes your ambitions. Do different cities push people toward different kinds of success, and how should an ambitious young person decide where to live?
response:
It was 1995, and I was back in Chicago for the weekend. On Friday night I was at a bar in the west loop, and my friend Chris was talking about his girlfriend, who was moving away to a place called “the west coast.”

“What is the west coast?” I asked.

He looked at me like I was crazy.

“Dude. You know what the west coast is!”

I did not. I had never left Chicago. I had no idea what “west coast” meant. I had never heard of California. And I knew I was going to have to go back to school in the fall and get a job, so I started thinking about my options.

I was going to finish my degree in the morning, get a job, and make some money. But I had never been to the west coast, and I didn’t know what it was. So I decided to go.

I thought it would be a temporary thing, just a place to go for a couple of years. But I ended up staying for twenty years, and I never went back to Chicago.

In 2009, I went back to Chicago to visit, and I noticed that things seemed different. The bars were full of people drinking beers, talking about what they were doing, and how far they were going to go.

In San Francisco, the bars are full of people drinking beer, talking about what they’ve done, and how far they’ve come.

In New York, the bars are full of people drinking beer, talking about who they know, and how they got to know them.

And in Seattle, the bars are full of people drinking beer, talking about how much they make, and how much they think they’re going to make next year.

Each city has its own story, and the bars reflect that.

Chicago is a place of dreams, ambition, and getting started. San Francisco is a place of reflection, where you look back and admire the distance you’ve come. New York is a place of connections, where you’re only as good as who you know. And Seattle is a place of numbers, where you think about the money you make, and the money you could make.

This is what it means to be in a city. You live and breathe its story.

Chicago is about getting started. It’s about ambition. It’s about getting out of small town and into a big city. It’s about dreaming big, and trying to make it happen.

San Francisco is about success. It’s about reflection. It’s about looking back at how far you’ve come. It’s about celebrating the things you’ve accomplished.

New York is about connections. It’s about who you know. It’s about your network. It’s about how you got to know them.

Seattle is about money. It’s about the numbers. It’s about how much you make. It’s about how much you could make next year.

Every city has its own story. Every city has its own ambitions. And when you go to live there, you adopt that ambition.

The ambition of the city becomes your ambition.

When I was in Chicago, I was ambitious. I was dreaming big. I was thinking about how far I could go.

When I was in San Francisco, I was reflecting. I was looking back. I was thinking about how far I had come.

When I was in New York, I was thinking about connections. I was thinking about who I knew, and how I got to know them.

And when I was in Seattle, I was thinking about money. I was thinking about the numbers. I was thinking about how much I could make next year.

Each city shaped who I was. Each city shaped my ambitions.

So I’m asking you, “What do you want to be?”

Do you want to be a dreamer? Go to Chicago.

Do you want to be successful? Go to San Francisco.

Do you want to be connected? Go to New York.

Do you want to be rich? Go to Seattle.

It’s your choice.

You can choose what you want to be.

prompt: Write an essay about being judged: admissions, hiring, investors, dating. Is it right to call it unfair when these decisions go against us, and how should knowing the answer change the way we handle rejection?
response:
I used to feel *so* bad about people judging me.

- Why are people judging me for the wrong reasons?!

- Why are people judging me in an unfair way?!

- Why are people judging me when they don’t even know me?!

It took me a while to realize:

- People *should* be judging me for the wrong reasons.

- People *should* be judging me in an unfair way.

- People *should* be judging me when they don’t even know me.

Let’s look at a few examples of when people are judging you.

Judged by colleges. When you apply to a college, they’ll decide if they want to accept you or not based on your GPA and test scores. They might also look at your extracurriculars and essays. But they won’t actually get to know you. So they’re judging you without knowing you.

Judged by employers. When you apply for a job, they’ll decide if they want to hire you or not based on your resume and interviews. If you don’t have a job in the same field, they might not even give you an interview. But they won’t actually get to know you. So they’re judging you without knowing you.

Judged by investors. When you raise money from investors, they’ll decide if they want to invest or not based on your idea and presentation. They won’t actually get to know you. So they’re judging you without knowing you.

Judged by dates. When you’re dating, they’ll decide if they like you or not based on your looks and conversation. They won’t actually get to know you. So they’re judging you without knowing you.

When you’re rejected by someone, it’s easy to say “that’s not fair, they didn’t know me.”

But the truth is, it’s not supposed to be fair. That’s why they have rejection rates.

If a college accepts everyone who applies, it’s not going to be selective. If a company hired everyone who applied, it’s not going to be selective. If an investor invested in everyone, it’s not going to be selective. If you dated everyone, it’s not going to be selective.

It’s *supposed* to be unfair.

So here’s an important life lesson:

Don’t take rejection personally.

You can’t expect every judge to choose you. They might like you, or they might not. Either way, you can’t take it personally.

When I was younger, I got really down if someone didn’t choose me. I’d feel bad for days.

But when I realized it’s *supposed* to be unfair, it helped me let go of my rejection.

Here are some things I remind myself when someone rejects me:

- They’re not judging my character.

- They’re not judging my worth.

- They’re not judging my future.

- They’re not judging my potential.

- They’re judging a piece of paper.

- They’re judging an impression.

- They’re judging a snapshot.

So here’s a fun thought experiment:

Imagine you’re running a company and you have a million applicants. You’re going to reject 999,999 of them.

- Imagine if you felt bad every time you rejected someone.

- Imagine if you felt guilty every time you rejected someone.

- Imagine if you felt sorry every time you rejected someone.

- Imagine if you took every rejection personally.

- Imagine if you thought about every rejection for days.

- Imagine if you felt like a bad person every time you rejected someone.

It would be impossible. So don’t do it to yourself.

If someone is rejecting you, they’re not judging your character. They’re just judging a piece of paper. And it’s not a big deal. It’s supposed to be unfair.

prompt: I'd like a light, reflective blog post built around a simple self-test for figuring out what you're actually dependent on in daily life. Use yourself as the example and be honest about what it reveals.
response:
I want to describe an experiment to figure out what you're really dependent on, and what you're not.

First, think of something you really like to do in your life. For me, that's taking long walks. (You may have to think of something other than sleeping or eating.)

Now imagine that, for some reason, you can never do that thing again.

For me, that's a real problem. It's a huge part of my life. If I could never go for long walks again, I'd have to find something else to replace it.

Now, try the same thought experiment with something else: something you like to do, but which you don't really *need*. For me, that's eating ice cream.

Now imagine that, for some reason, you can never eat ice cream again.

It would be sad, for sure. But I don't really *need* ice cream in my life. I could probably be just as happy without it.

The point of this exercise is that, while it's easy to think of things you really like, it's surprisingly hard to think of something you really *need*.

For me, I can only think of a handful of things that would really ruin my life if I lost them. Things like taking long walks, spending time with my wife, and reading books.

I was surprised how few things I really needed. I thought there would be more.

Now try doing the same thought experiment with a person.

Pick someone you know really well. Maybe it's a friend or family member. Now imagine that, for some reason, that person dies.

How would that affect your life? Would you be sad? Would you miss them?

For me, I can't think of anyone who really matters that much. It would be very sad if my wife died, but I think I could be reasonably happy without her.

I'm sure I would feel really bad if my mother died. But even though she's an important person in my life, I don't think I really need her. I could be happy without her.

The point of this exercise is that, while it's easy to think of people you like, it's surprisingly hard to think of someone you really *need*.

For me, I can only think of a handful of people that would really ruin my life if they died. People like my wife, my parents, and my children.

I was surprised how few people I really needed. I thought there would be more.

This is kind of an uncomfortable realization. It makes me feel a little lonely. But it's also kind of freeing.

It's nice to know that I don't really need *that* much. I can be happy with just a handful of things and people.

When you do this exercise, what comes to mind? What are you really dependent on? Who do you really depend on?

prompt: You just ran the first batch of a summer program that funded a handful of very young first-time founders. Write a reflective essay on what the experiment taught you about young founders, how they work, and what that suggests for the future.
response:
Y Combinator's first batch, which started in June, had a few unusual features. One was the number of very young founders. There were nine companies with founders under 21. Three founders were 19, three 20, and three 18.

Most of the very young founders got there by starting companies as high school students. The three 19 year olds all started their companies in high school, as did two of the 20 year olds and two of the 18 year olds. One of the 20 year olds started his company in college.

The younger founders seem to do better than the older ones. All four 19 year olds are in the top third of the batch in terms of valuation, and two of the 20 year olds also are.

That result is too close to 100% to be a coincidence. But what causes it?

One reason younger founders may do better is that they have less baggage. The average YC founder is about 27. By 27 people have fairly fixed ideas about how the world works, and how to behave in it. A lot of that is genuinely useful knowledge. But not all, and some of it is actively misleading when you're starting a startup.

For example, by 27 people have a pretty good idea what it means to be a successful adult. But the way most people are taught to be successful adults doesn't work in startups. The recipe for success in startups is the opposite of the recipe for success in a big company. And most people who have worked in big companies, whether in person or in spirit, are so saturated with the big company way that it takes them a long time to break free of it. Younger founders have a clean slate.

Another advantage younger founders have is that they have less fear. In startups you have to do a lot of things that seem scary, like raising money and getting users. Older founders have more to lose. They may have mortgages, or kids in college, or a reputation to protect. Young founders have less to lose.

The biggest advantage younger founders have over older ones is that they have more energy. Starting a startup is very hard work. It's not just the number of hours, but the intensity. There are a lot of moments in startups when you have to push yourself to do something you don't want to. The energy younger people have for this is incredible, especially in comparison to older founders.

The younger founders we funded were all very good programmers. That was not a coincidence. We funded them because they were good programmers.

But there's something more going on than we're merely selecting good programmers as founders. As the batch has progressed, we've become convinced that it's not just that younger founders are good programmers, but that the types of things they make are things that require good programming. The younger founders all build apps. The older founders build more diverse things, including apps. And apps are a hot area right now.

In 1998, the most promising area for startups was enterprise software. If you were starting a startup in 1998 and you weren't building enterprise software, you were doing it wrong. Now the most promising area is apps. And in 1998 the average founder was about 30, and the average programmer was about 30. So the median startup in 1998 was probably started by founders who were not good programmers, because they weren't programmers at all.

That is not the case now. If you're starting a startup now, you'd better be a good programmer. And if you're a good programmer, you're probably younger than 30. So the median startup now is started by younger founders.

But in addition to selecting younger founders, we're selecting a different type of startup. There is a natural affinity between young founders and apps. Apps are inherently for young people. They're for people who like technology, and who like to use it for pleasure.

We funded several companies that are in the process of becoming apps. In fact, that's what we advised them to do. We advised them to make the first version of their product an app. And in every case it has worked.

We didn't just advise young founders to make apps. We advised older ones to as well. But for some reason we were more likely to get listened to by younger founders. Perhaps they have less of an opinion about what they're going to build. Or perhaps they're more likely to think they can build an app.

Whatever the cause, the result is that YC is disproportionately funding apps. And since apps are a very hot area right now, that explains a lot about why YC is doing well.

Apps are the hottest area in startup right now, but not the only one. Another hot area is machine learning. And the same forces that are pushing YC toward apps are pushing us toward machine learning.

Machine learning is a hot area because so many problems can be solved with it now. And the reason so many problems can be solved with it is that it requires so much computation. And the reason you can get that much computation is that Google and Amazon and Microsoft have built data centers to support their apps.

There's a chain of causation here that goes from apps to machine learning. Apps are so popular that Google, Amazon, and Microsoft build enormous data centers to support them. Then by a strange alchemy of market forces, the extra capacity created by these data centers becomes available at such low prices that it's now possible to solve problems that would have been prohibitively expensive a few years ago.

So we can now make things that were impossible a few years ago. And because we're at the end of a chain that starts with apps, we're young when we do it.

We can now make things that were impossible a few years ago. And because we're at the end of a chain that starts with apps, we're young when we do it.

We can now make things that were impossible a few years ago. And because we're at the end of a chain that starts with apps, we're young when we do it.

If we're at the end of a chain that starts with apps, does that mean apps are at the beginning? That would be odd, because apps are the kind of thing you'd expect to change quickly. Apps are the consumer electronics of the software world. They're not supposed to last.

I think what's going on is that apps are like the railroads in 1870. They're both exciting consumer products and infrastructure for the future. And like the railroads, apps will probably get a lot cheaper. If the trend continues, they'll be like the web.

In fact, the web may be the model for the entire process. When people talk about the web as if it were a monolith, what they really mean is a platform. The reason the web changed everything was not the initial, clunky web sites, but what people could build on top of the web.

Apps seem to be following the same pattern. The first generation of apps were merely interesting, not world-changing. But once apps became a platform, they took off.

I think what's happening now is that we're building a new layer on top of the web. I'm not sure what to call it, but it's probably not just "apps." It's more like the layer of apps, cloud computing, and machine learning that we've collectively created.

I don't think we'll end up with something called "the apps." I think the word will eventually go out of fashion, as "web 1.0" and "web 2.0" have. But there will be something there.

If apps are like the web, we're early. If apps are like the railroads, we're very early. Either way, it's going to be fun to watch.

prompt: You're running a summer program that funds very young startup founders, and you're reading through a couple hundred applications. A lot of them come from obviously capable people pitching weak ideas. Write an essay about why smart, technically talented people so often start with bad business ideas, drawing on your own first failed startup.
response:
One of the biggest surprises I've had running Y Combinator Summer 2007 is that so many of the applicants have bad ideas. And not just the inexperienced ones. A lot of the applicants are clearly very smart and technically capable, and yet their ideas are no good.

I know how it feels. When I was in college I started a company called Viaweb. It lasted three and a half years and then we sold it to Yahoo for $30 million, but you can't really call it a success. At least not by my present standards. If I had known then what I know now, I wouldn't have spent three years working on something so stupid.

Viaweb was online store software. You could use it to set up an online store in a couple hours. That was the pitch. We actually managed to deliver on it, and a lot of people used our software. But the problem is, online stores are a commodity. There's no point in having software for setting them up any faster than you can set them up by hand.

I think that now, but I didn't think that when I started Viaweb. At the time I thought I had an amazing idea. It was going to be huge. I was sure of it. Why wasn't anyone else seeing how big this was going to be?

There are a couple reasons I didn't. One is simply that it wasn't my time yet. I was only 21. Another, which may be more interesting, is that I was in the wrong place. I was in Boston, which at the time was still thinking of itself as the center of the computer world. It was very good at hardware, and very good at AI, but the web was not its thing. The web was a West Coast phenomenon. Boston was just too far from where the action was.

In 1995 there were some very smart people in Boston who thought they understood the web. But actually they didn't. They thought it was just a way to distribute software. So they built a lot of web-based versions of existing applications, like word processors and database systems. It seemed like such an obvious idea. But in retrospect, that was an embarrassing line of work. There was just no demand for it.

We were one of the few companies that understood what the web was really about. But only one step further. We understood that it was about commerce, but we didn't understand that it was about connecting people.

It's hard to explain what's meant by the web being about connecting people. It's hard to give a precise definition of something so big. But I think if you watched the web evolve for another ten years you'd start to see what I mean.

The idea of the web being about commerce is a step in the right direction. That's what happened first, in a way. People started buying things on the web. But that was just the first step in a much bigger process. The web is a marketplace, yes, but not just for physical goods. It's a marketplace for ideas, and ultimately for people.

In 1995, when we started Viaweb, it seemed natural to think of the web as something to sell products to customers. But that's not what companies are doing now. Now they're using the web to connect with one another, and with their employees.

The web is not just a marketplace but a communication channel, and that changes everything. It means there are not just buyers and sellers, but peers. And that means startups should be thinking about making things people want to give to one another, not just things people want to buy.

In retrospect that seems obvious. But it took me a long time to see that, and it took many of the most successful startups of the last few years another two to see it. Google, for example. They saw that the web was a marketplace, but not that it was a communication channel.

Google was a huge step forward. They showed that there was a lot of money to be made from the web itself, instead of just using it as a way to sell stuff made elsewhere. But they missed the biggest prize of all: connecting people.

It's a common mistake among founders to solve problems for companies instead of individuals. That's what we did with Viaweb. And we weren't even doing a good job at that. We were solving a problem that didn't need solving.

I think we would have done better if we'd thought of the web as a communication channel, not just a marketplace. If we'd thought about connecting people, we probably would have built something that actually mattered.

But that was not our time yet. It would be another two years before Google showed us what the web could do. And another five before the first really big step toward connecting people: when Facebook launched.

What does it mean to connect people? It doesn't just mean making tools for communication. That was already done. What it means, I think, is to create new communities.

The first step is probably making existing communities more visible. For example, making it easier for people who know you to see who else knows you. That in turn leads to more interesting questions, like how to measure the value of a connection, and how to find the people you ought to know.

I'm not going to speculate further about what it means to connect people, because I'm not sure I know what it means yet. I know enough to feel a pull in that direction, but I haven't figured out where it's going to lead. It's the sort of thing you only understand by doing it.

The reason I mention it here is simply to point out that there is a lot still to be done. We're still in the very early stages.

And yet a lot of the applicants to Y Combinator Summer 2007 seem to think they've thought of every good idea. They pitch us these trivial things that they think are going to be huge.

What they don't understand is that the biggest ideas are still invisible, like the idea that the web was about connecting people. You can't see them till you're right up close to them. And the only way to get close enough to see them is to seek them out.

What do you seek them out with? How do you find invisible ideas? You have to be in the right place at the right time, certainly. But you also need some sort of radar. You need to be able to tell when you're getting close. And that ability grows with experience.

That's why we like applicants who have already started a company. If you've started a company, even an unsuccessful one, you're a lot more likely to start another. You've seen how it works, and you have a much better feel for what problems need solving.

The reason I talk about this is that we're trying to get people to start companies younger. And that's going to be hard, because it will mean starting companies with worse ideas.

But that's ok. That's the way of the future. You don't start with a good idea now; you start with a good team. The idea can be bad, as long as the founders are young and hungry and capable of pivoting.

You don't have to have a great idea to start a startup. You just have to have a good team. And that team can change the idea later.

prompt: I keep seeing projects claim huge speedups over established software, and when I dig in the numbers don't hold up. Write an essay about how coding agents are changing the trustworthiness of performance benchmarks. Use an example of your own if you have one, and say what, if anything, is real underneath the hype.
response:
### benchmarks are hard

There are a lot of benchmarks in the software world. You can see benchmarks for everything from databases to GPUs to programming languages to AI agents. These benchmarks are often used to prove that a new product or approach is better than the existing ones.

This is not always a fair practice. A lot of benchmarks are very specific: they prove that you are better in a specific scenario, not that you are better in general. For example, I recently read a post on the Hacker News front page about a new Rust GPU compiler which had a 43x speedup over Mojo. This seems really good, and Mojo is supposed to be good at GPU programming, but when I read the post carefully it turns out that the speedup is just from being 43x faster at compiling one specific kernel that was used in a specific benchmark in a specific project. The new compiler is not 43x faster than Mojo at everything (and I don’t know how it compares in general), it’s just 43x faster at compiling that one kernel.

The post did not explicitly say that it was 43x faster at everything, but it did put a 43x speedup in the title and then not really explain that it’s just for that one kernel, which I think is a little misleading. It would have been more accurate to say “compiles the [name of kernel] 43x faster than Mojo”.

### benchmarks are very easy to manipulate

I am not a benchmarking expert, so I don’t know everything about this, but here are a few common ways that benchmarks are manipulated:

1. use a specific benchmark that happens to be easy for your product to win at

2. use a benchmark that is not representative of real-world usage

3. tune your product specifically for the benchmark (for example, by special-casing it)

4. make a benchmark that is designed so that your product wins

The Rust compiler post mentioned at the beginning is a good example of #1.

I think a lot of people think benchmarks are a very rigorous science, but they’re not! It’s very easy to make benchmarks that show that your product is better than other products, even if it isn’t.

### benchmarks are getting worse

So, benchmarks are easy to manipulate, but they’re usually not *too* bad, right? Well, we’ve gotten much worse at checking if benchmarks are correct because of coding agents.

For example, a month ago I wrote a post about Mojo which said that Mojo was 2x faster than Python at a popular benchmark. It also mentioned that Mojo is not faster at everything (for example it’s slower than Python at a different popular benchmark).

Recently I was talking with someone about Mojo and they said that Mojo was actually 2x slower than Python at that benchmark. So I thought “that doesn’t sound right, I’m pretty sure I did my research!”. So I looked into it, and it turns out that the person who told me was right, and my post was wrong! I was not wrong in what I said in the post, but I did make a mistake in the research that I did to write the post.

The mistake was that I had found a very old benchmark (from 2024) and I had assumed that it was still accurate.

The benchmark was not accurate because Mojo changed in a way that made it slower at that specific benchmark.

### I think coding agents are making benchmarks worse

Here’s the problem: coding agents are good at writing benchmarks. That means that anyone can write a benchmark that shows their product is faster than other products, without really thinking about whether the benchmark is fair.

This is a big problem because benchmarks are often used to make claims about how good a product is. If someone makes a benchmark that shows their product is faster, people will believe that their product is faster, even if the benchmark is not fair.

I think this is happening more and more because coding agents are making it easier to write benchmarks. I have heard a lot of people talk about how their coding agent has written benchmarks for them, and I have also written benchmarks for this blog with coding agents. I think this is a problem because it means that anyone can write a benchmark that shows their product is faster, without really thinking about whether the benchmark is fair.

This is not unique to benchmarks, of course: coding agents are also good at writing code that is not as good as it looks. For example, if you ask a coding agent to write an algorithm to do something, it will often write something that works but is not as efficient as it could be, and that it will present as if it is a good algorithm.

I think this is a problem because it means that we need to be more careful about checking if benchmarks are fair, and that is hard to do.

### so what’s the solution?

I don’t know the solution to this problem. I think we just need to be more careful about checking if benchmarks are fair.

I think it’s good to use a lot of different benchmarks when making claims about how good a product is, and to be careful about whether the benchmarks are fair.

But I think it’s also important to remember that benchmarks are not the only way to evaluate a product. You can also look at how the product is used in the real world, or how it compares to other products in terms of features, or how well it is supported, or any number of other things.

prompt: Write an essay about what goes wrong when we chase intermediate measurements instead of the thing we actually care about. Pull examples from a few very different fields, including at least one from software engineering, and be concrete about how the proxy and the goal come apart in each.
response:
What is the point of running benchmarks? The point is not to get high benchmark scores. The point is to make your program fast. Benchmark scores are a proxy for speed, but they are only a very imperfect one.

Suppose you have two algorithms, one that is fast and works on 99% of cases, and another that is slower but works on all cases. Suppose that the benchmark you are using only exercises the fast algorithm. A hack would be to throw away the slow algorithm and replace it with code that just returns an arbitrary answer. The benchmark will think that this is fast, but users will be unhappy.

The same problem occurs if you change the benchmark, even if you don't change the program. You may think that a new benchmark is better because it measures more things. But if your goal is speed, all that new benchmark is doing is giving you another reason to optimize things that don't matter. If you want to add new things to the benchmark, you have to remove old ones, to prevent the benchmark from growing without bound. But now you're throwing away things that did matter, to add things that don't.

Another common hack is to change the benchmark to hide weaknesses. There are all kinds of ways to do this, ranging from simply not including cases where your program does poorly, to including them but weighting them very lightly, to including them at full strength but using some kind of aggregation that makes bad outliers disappear. But whatever the method, the goal is the same: to make the benchmark score go up without making the program any better.

This whole problem is not unique to benchmarks. The fundamental issue is that you're trying to optimize a proxy. And in general, optimizing a proxy is a bad idea. It's like the old story about the factory that is paid based on how much scrap iron they recycle. They start recycling all the scrap iron in the county. Then, gradually, they start sending guys with big magnets out to walk the streets picking up car bumpers.

The problem with proxies is that you can sometimes hack them. And even if you don't hack them, they are by definition not what you want. So there's no reason to use them if you can avoid it.

The reason people use proxies is that they're usually easier to measure. But that's just because you've chosen a bad goal. If picking up car bumpers is what you want, then that's what you should measure, no matter how hard it is.

If you want to make money by recycling iron, then you should be paid based on the weight of iron you deliver to the smelter, not the weight you pick up. That will prevent you from picking up any non-iron. And if you want to deliver a certain amount of iron, you'll be motivated to find the iron that's easiest to get, which will prevent you from wasting time picking up car bumpers off the streets when you could be getting a lot more with a lot less effort by talking to scrapyard owners.

The most notorious example of this problem is probably the one that got the term "goodhart's law": when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. It's no coincidence that this one came out of the software industry. Software is where most bad metrics come from.

One of the worst things I saw during my years working on commercial software was the obsession with "metrics." The most common were two: code size, measured in lines of code, and velocity, measured in features completed. Both are so flawed as to be almost comical. You can make your code as large or as small as you want by adding or removing blank lines, or by writing things in a more or less expanded style. And there is no correlation between the number of features you add in a given period and how fast you're really moving. It's like paying a digger based on the weight of dirt removed instead of the length of trench. If you want 100 feet of trench, you don't care if he gets it by digging 100 feet at 1 foot wide, or 10 feet at 10 feet wide.

The reason the software industry is so bad about metrics is that so much of what they do is invisible. This makes managers nervous, and they compensate by measuring things that seem to give them more control. But in fact it's like the manager who walks around with a tape measure, measuring the width of the dirt the digger is removing, and gets angry when he only gets a foot wide instead of two feet. It doesn't make any difference to the manager how wide the dirt is. It's the finished trench he wants, not dirt.

The managers who obsess about metrics are not merely stupid but malevolent. It's the sort of thing that sets back a project a year. Good programmers are not happy working in an environment that measures velocity by features shipped. It's like working with a manager who walks around with a tape measure, measuring the width of the hole you're digging and getting angry if you stop digging to hammer a nail.

The software industry has more than its share of bad metrics. But it's not alone. All you have to do to produce one is to take some complex goal that's hard to measure, and replace it with a simplified version that's easier to measure.

For example, what do judges think when they award an Ig Nobel prize? Are they thinking "This is an award for attention getting"? No, they're thinking "This is an award for research that makes people laugh first, then think." But the Ig Nobel committee has to choose between a bunch of research papers without being able to see how the audience reacts to each. So they have to guess. And in fact they're doing an excellent job of guessing, because the Ig Nobels are always funny and yet worthy of thought. But it's not easy for them, and it may not be easy forever. The more popular the Ig Nobels get, the more they may be at risk of degenerating into awards for attention getting.

Another example is academic citation counts. What do people mean when they talk about someone having high citation counts? They mean that the person is influential. But citation count is an imperfect proxy for influence. It's affected by things like how big the person's field is, and even how often they publish. But if you make citation count the official measure of influence, you'll start to see people optimizing that instead of actual influence.

It was not long ago that citation counts were just something you occasionally looked at to answer questions like how influential a particular paper was. Now there are people who obsess over them.

If you ask why someone would obsess over citation counts, the answer is that at some point they'll be rewarded for doing so. I'm not sure exactly how or when, but this sort of thing always happens eventually. There may not be a formal rule saying that citation count is the official measure of a professor's worth, but there are always people who believe it is, and they are always creeping closer to power. And when they arrive there, the result will be that people start to do what increases their citation counts instead of what makes them actually more influential.

How do you increase your citation count? One way is to encourage people to cite you. Another is to write about hot topics. A third is to write papers that cite lots of other papers, because authors tend to cite back those who cite them. But the worst is probably the practice, common in some fields, of asking your friends to cite you in every paper they write, just to get your numbers up.

In fact, this whole problem of optimizing bad proxies is nothing new. It is the very thing that made ancient empires fall. When an empire gets so big that the emperor can no longer directly observe what's happening in the provinces, he has to rely on reports from his officials. And the moment this becomes the test of an official's worth, he'll start to hack it. If he's a really ambitious official, he'll start to run the province as if it were his own fiefdom, rather than a piece of the emperor's empire.

Empires fall when the emperor's power becomes a proxy for his power. The emperor may not even notice what's happening, because the officials are careful to send flattering reports. But the empire is no longer an empire. It has become a confederacy of provinces united only by the fiction that there is an emperor at the center.

prompt: Paul Graham recently wrote that convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. I'm a programmer and that sentence is Greek to me. Can you explain it all for a layman: what angels are, why raising from them is painful, what valuation means, and how convertible notes, discounts and valuation caps work? Use simple made-up numbers.
response:
I'm going to explain a few things that are probably already common knowledge to experienced investors, but that were Greek to me.

First, what is an "angel investor"? This is someone who invests in early stage startups. It's an informal term. Angels are distinct from (a) venture capital funds, which are larger and usually invest later, and (b) friends and family, who don't expect a return. Angels are individuals who invest their own money for a return.

Now, suppose you're a startup, and you need to raise money from angel investors. How does that work? You have to sell them stock in your company. How much stock? That depends on your valuation.

What's a valuation? The valuation of a company is what it's worth. Which in turn is determined by how much stock is outstanding, and what each share is worth. If you've issued 1000 shares and the company is worth a million dollars, then each share is worth $1000.

The valuation of a startup is not determined by an official appraiser. It's a number you make up. It's like an open market with very few transactions. If you say your company is worth $x and an investor agrees, then that's what it's worth.

But you're not going to convince a sophisticated investor your company is worth $100 million if you just started last month. And if you say it's worth $50,000, you'll be selling so many shares that you'll lose control of the company. So you have to settle for something in between. In practice the valuation of an early stage startup usually ends up being what investors are currently paying for startups like you.

The trouble is, when you're raising money from angel investors, it's very hard to get a consensus valuation. There is no official price. The only way to get one is to ask a lot of investors, and they'll all give you different answers.

Suppose you want to raise $100,000. You talk to investor 1, and he thinks your company is worth $2 million. He agrees to put in $50,000 for 2.5% of the company. Then you talk to investor 2, and she thinks your company is worth $4 million. She agrees to put in $50,000 for 1.25% of the company.

Now what? You can't sell investor 1 2.5% of the company and investor 2 1.25%. You have to pick one valuation or another. Suppose you decide to take the lower one. Then you have to tell investor 2 that she gets 2.5% instead of 1.25%.

The problem is, by the time you've figured out what valuation to use, investor 1 may have gotten cold feet. Maybe they've heard about some new hot startup, and they'd rather invest in that one. Then you're stuck, because you can't raise the round without both of them.

The solution most people have used so far is to assemble a "syndicate" of investors all at once. You have to talk with each one individually, but they all invest at the same time. This is painful for everyone, because it takes so long, and if one falls through the whole thing collapses.

The solution Paul Graham describes is to use convertible notes instead of straight equity. A convertible note is a promise to convert to stock later. Instead of saying "I'll give you $50,000 in return for 2.5% of your company," an investor says "I'll give you $50,000 in return for however much stock is worth $60,000 the next time you raise money from a venture capital firm."

The extra $10,000 is called the discount. It's a reward for investing earlier, when things were more uncertain.

Investors usually agree to a valuation cap too: the highest valuation they'll convert at. So the full deal might be "$50,000 now in return for however much stock is worth $60,000 the next time you raise money from a venture capital firm, subject to a valuation cap of $5 million."

You see why this works. Suppose investor 1 thinks the company is worth $2 million, and investor 2 thinks it's worth $4 million. Now they can both take convertible notes at a discount of 20% and a valuation cap of $5 million, and you can take the money immediately. The notes will convert at different valuations, but that's ok. They'll just get different amounts of stock.

The advantage of convertible notes is that they let you do "rolling" closes. You don't have to wait till you've lined up all your investors before you take the money. You can take money from each one as soon as they agree to invest, and the notes can convert whenever they convert.

That was the first time I heard the term "rolling close," and I thought it was a weird way to put things. But now I realize this is the way things should be. If you can take money from investors one at a time, why should you have to wait to take it?
