prompt: Why do deep neural networks work so well? I'd like a blog post that tries to answer this through the lens of natural language processing results, aimed at readers who know some machine learning but haven't followed NLP research closely.
response:
This post is an attempt to answer the question: why do deep neural networks work so well? It is a bit of a long shot, but I think we can find some evidence in the recent advances in natural language processing.

First, let’s review the situation.

### Why are deep neural networks so good?

Deep neural networks are good for several reasons. For one, they’re flexible. A neural network has a very simple computational unit (the perceptron), and by combining many of these units, we can get a model that can fit an incredibly wide variety of functions.

But that alone doesn’t get us very far. It’s easy to come up with other models that can fit just as wide a variety of functions. So why are neural networks so good?

I think one key reason they work is that the building block of a neural network – the perceptron – has properties that are well suited to machine learning. In particular, it’s simple enough that we can train it very quickly.

To see why that matters, imagine that we want to learn a function that looks like this:

You could try to learn this function with a model that has a lot of parameters. For example, you could start with a polynomial with 10,000 terms. But the problem is that with so many parameters, you’ll have a very complex optimization landscape. There will be a lot of local minima, and it will be hard to find the right values for the parameters.

Or, you could start with a simpler model – say, a polynomial with 5 terms. But then you’ll run into the opposite problem: the model will be too limited to capture the structure of the function.

But the neural network gives us something like the best of both worlds: it has the flexibility to capture the complex functions we might want to learn, but its simple structure means that we can train it really quickly. And this, in turn, means that we can create very flexible models without having to worry too much about the difficulty of training.

The perceptron is not the only possible building block for neural networks, but it is one of the most effective. For example, convolutional networks are very popular for computer vision. These networks use a different kind of building block that is very well-suited to images. So there’s a lot to be said for using building blocks that are well-suited to a particular problem. But the perceptron, with its simplicity, is a really good default.

### Why does the perceptron work?

So why is the perceptron so effective? The perceptron is so simple – it just adds up the inputs and then applies a nonlinearity – that I don’t think we should expect it to work. So if it does work, there must be something about the data we’re trying to learn.

In the case of computer vision, we can understand why the perceptron works. Images have a lot of local structure – a cat has ears and eyes and whiskers, for example – and the perceptron is good at discovering this local structure.

But what about text? Why do neural networks work so well for natural language processing tasks?

### Word embeddings

A major breakthrough in NLP was the discovery of word embeddings.

Word embeddings are a way of representing words as vectors. These vectors have some interesting properties. For example, the vector for “king” is approximately equal to the vector for “man” plus the vector for “queen” minus the vector for “woman”.

One way to discover these word embeddings is with a neural network. The word embeddings are part of the parameters of the network. But we don’t need to use a neural network to get the word embeddings. We can also extract the word vectors from a linear model, which is a lot faster to train. In fact, this is the way that most people get word embeddings.

But the word embeddings are a bit magical. How come we can represent words as vectors? How come we can do arithmetic with them?

To understand why this works, let’s think about the problem of language modeling.

### Language modeling

Language modeling is the task of predicting what word comes next in a sentence. For example, given the sentence “We had fish and _____ for dinner,” a language model would try to predict that the next word is “chips.”

It turns out that we can solve this problem quite well with a linear model. If we take the vectors for “fish” and “and”, add them together, and then take the dot product with the vectors for a bunch of possible words, we can find the word that’s most likely to come next.

But this doesn’t explain why we can do arithmetic with word vectors. So let’s think about the problem a little bit more.

### Language modeling is easy

One of the most striking things about the language modeling task is how easy it is.

For example, if you want to predict the word that comes next in a sentence, you can often get away with just looking at the last word. For example, if the sentence is “We had fish and _____ for dinner,” all you need to know is the last word (“and”) to predict the next word (“chips”).

This seems surprising. How come you only need to know one word to predict the next?

The answer is that the structure of language is very local. There are a lot of patterns in language that only involve a couple of words, like “fish and chips”, “rock and roll”, and “salt and pepper.”

The language modeling task is a lot like the computer vision task. Just as images have a lot of local structure, so does language.

This is the key to understanding why the perceptron works in NLP. It’s good at discovering local structure. And because language has a lot of local structure, it works well for NLP.

### How to learn language

So how do we learn language? Well, it’s a lot like learning computer vision.

First, we learn all the local patterns. For example, we learn that “fish” is often followed by “and”, which is often followed by “chips.” We also learn that “rock” is often followed by “and”, which is often followed by “roll.”

Then, we combine these local patterns to make more complicated patterns. For example, we can combine the patterns “fish and chips” and “rock and roll” to make a pattern for things that go together.

And so on. At each level, we combine the local patterns to make more complicated patterns.

The perceptron is well suited to learning local patterns, and so it is well suited to learning language.

### Language has no global structure

The last thing I want to mention is that language doesn’t have much global structure.

For example, in computer vision, we can often understand an image just by looking at its parts. If you see a bunch of cat-like parts (ears, eyes, whiskers, etc.), you can be pretty sure that the image is of a cat.

But in language, it’s much harder to understand a sentence just by looking at its parts. For example, the sentence “I’ll take my coffee black, no sugar, and no milk” has no obvious local patterns. There’s nothing obvious that links “coffee” with “black”, “sugar”, and “milk”.

To understand a sentence like this one, we need to understand the global structure of the sentence. We need to understand that “coffee”, “black”, “sugar”, and “milk” are all related to the topic of making coffee. And then we need to understand that the sentence is saying that the speaker wants their coffee without any of the usual additions (black, sugar, milk).

But if language doesn’t have any global structure, how come deep neural networks work so well for NLP?

Well, I think it’s because there’s actually a lot of global structure in language. It’s just not the kind of global structure that we usually think of.

I think that the global structure of language is really about how words are used. For example, the word “coffee” is often used in sentences about making coffee, but it’s also often used in sentences about drinking coffee. And the word “black” is often used in sentences about color, but it’s also often used in sentences about making coffee.

So the global structure of language is really about how words are used in different contexts. And I think that this is what deep neural networks are learning.

### Conclusion

So, to recap:

- Deep neural networks work well because they’re flexible and easy to train.

- The perceptron is well suited to discovering local structure.

- Language has a lot of local structure, so neural networks work well for NLP.

prompt: Every time something terrible happens online, people demand that hosting and payment companies cut off the people involved. Write a short personal essay on why that line is harder to draw than it looks.

This, too, seemed like a great idea.

Now, here’s what’s interesting about this.

You’ve probably noticed that when something bad happens on the Internet, people often suggest that payment processors, hosting providers, and Google should deny services to the people involved.

But it turns out that’s not so easy.

Payment processors like Visa and Mastercard, as well as the companies that process payments for those processors, have a very difficult job. They have to be careful that they’re not processing payments for companies that are doing something illegal. But it’s not always obvious when they’re doing something illegal. And if they shut off a client who’s not really doing anything wrong, then they’ll lose a lot of money and they’ll lose credibility with other merchants.

And if you don’t shut off a client who’s doing something illegal, then people will notice that you’re doing something wrong, and you’ll lose credibility with other merchants.

And then there are hosting companies, who have a similar problem. They have to be careful that they’re not hosting sites that are doing something illegal, but it’s not always obvious when a site is doing something illegal. And if they shut off a client who’s not really doing anything wrong, then they’ll lose a lot of money and they’ll lose credibility with other customers.

And if you don’t shut off a client who’s doing something illegal, then people will notice that you’re doing something wrong, and you’ll lose credibility with other customers.

And then there are companies like Google, who have to be careful that they’re not indexing sites that are doing something illegal, but it’s not always obvious when a site is doing something illegal. And if they shut off a client who’s not really doing anything wrong, then they’ll lose a lot of money and they’ll lose credibility with other customers.

And if you don’t shut off a client who’s doing something illegal, then people will notice that you’re doing something wrong, and you’ll lose credibility with other customers.

I think this is really important to keep in mind. It’s easy to say that companies should deny services to people who are doing something illegal, but it’s not that simple.

A lot of companies have tried to make it so that it’s really hard to do something illegal on the Internet. But there are still a lot of bad actors, and there will probably always be bad actors. And even though a lot of companies do their best to keep bad actors out, it’s not always easy to keep them out.

prompt: A Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that's offensive to minority groups, more than any other generation. That seems odd for the most online, most tolerant generation. Write a blog post trying to make sense of it.
response:
A recent Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that offends minority groups. This is higher than any other generation, and higher than any other country except China.

This is surprising, because millennials are the generation that’s most online, the most tolerant, and the most likely to believe “we’re all different, and that’s okay”. And yet they’re also the generation most likely to want government censorship, even though they’re the generation that invented free speech on the Internet, which should have helped them understand how important free speech is.

I’m going to try to make sense of this by splitting the question into two components: what people think about minorities, and what people think about censorship.

I think the first part of this is pretty straightforward. Millennials are more tolerant of minorities than any other generation, and that’s probably why they’re more likely to want the government to protect minorities from offensive speech.

The other half of the question, “what people think about censorship” is a bit more complicated. A common way of thinking about censorship is “I want censorship if it protects me, but not if it limits me”. This is what people usually mean when they say “free speech is just an excuse for bullies to oppress minorities”.

A more sophisticated way of thinking about censorship is “censorship is a slippery slope, if we allow it to restrict some people then it will always end up restricting me”.

I think millennials have the first way of thinking about censorship. They’re very tolerant, so they don’t feel like their own speech will be restricted. They’re also the most online generation, so they’re the most exposed to the worst effects of free speech and the most likely to see it as oppressive.

So even though they’re the generation that most understands free speech, they’re also the generation most likely to want censorship.

I’m not saying millennials are wrong. It’s a good thing that they’re more tolerant and understand free speech better than past generations. I’m just saying that this doesn’t mean they’re less likely to support censorship. In fact, it might do the opposite.

I think this is a useful insight, because it’s a common mistake to think that people who are more tolerant are less likely to support censorship. This is not true. People who are more tolerant are less likely to be restricted by censorship, but they’re also less likely to want to restrict others, so there’s no net effect.

prompt: Marco Arment funding his Overcast app through patronage set off a big argument about whether only people with famous personal brands can live off crowdfunding. Write a short essay on what crowdfunding has actually proven, and what might come after it.
response:
Marco Arment announced that he’s going to try making money off his app Overcast through a combination of donations and subscription patronage, in the same way that I’ve been making money off my newsletter and books. It was a big deal, because he’s one of the most well-known app developers in the world, and because this is a pretty unusual business model for an app.

The announcement set off a big debate on Twitter about whether crowdfunding is an effective business model, and who it’s effective for. The debate is a bit confusing and I think I have some insights that might help clarify it.

### 1. Crowdfunding is an experiment, not a finished product

The most fundamental insight I have is that crowdfunding is not a finished product. It is an experiment.

There have been a lot of experiments in the software industry over the last 20 years. Some of them have succeeded and changed the industry permanently. For example, open source is a big experiment that has succeeded. We know that open source is here to stay, and we don’t even think of it as an “experiment” anymore.

Other experiments have failed, or have not succeeded yet. For example, the idea of selling software as a physical product, like a CD or DVD, has failed. (We still have to use the phrase “physical product” because it’s no longer the default way of selling software.)

But other experiments are still in progress. For example, “freemium” is an experiment that hasn’t quite finished yet. It’s certainly been a big part of the mobile app industry. But now it seems to be in decline, and I think that in the future, we’ll look back at freemium in the same way that we look back at selling software on physical media.

There are a lot of other experiments going on. For example, the idea of “bootstrapping” a company — meaning, starting a company without any venture capital funding — is a big experiment that is still in progress. And crowdfunding is also an ongoing experiment.

When we talk about a business model like “freemium”, or “bootstrapping”, or “crowdfunding”, we’re talking about a set of experiments that are still in progress. They’re not finished. We don’t know yet which of these experiments will succeed or fail.

### 2. The experiment is about more than just making money

The most common complaint I hear about crowdfunding is that it’s hard to make money with it. But in fact, this experiment is about more than just making money.

When you ask people to donate to your project, or to become a patron, you’re not just asking them for money. You’re asking them to be part of your community, and to help make it grow.

If people are donating money to you, that means they are happy with your work and they want to support you and make it possible for you to continue doing it. It means they’re willing to help you make a difference, and to be part of something bigger than themselves.

The way I think about crowdfunding is not just “I’m going to ask people to pay money to me.” It’s more like “I’m going to create a community of people who believe in what I do and want to support it.”

This is a bigger experiment than just “is it possible to make money this way?” It’s more like “is it possible to create a community of people who believe in what I do and want to support it?”

This is a really interesting question, because it’s not just about making money. It’s about building a community. And we don’t know yet what this will look like.

### 3. The current model doesn’t work for everyone

One of the most common complaints I hear about crowdfunding is that it only works for people who are already famous.

This is true. It’s much easier to get people to donate to your project if you’re already well-known.

The reason is that there’s a chicken and egg problem with crowdfunding. If you’re not famous, it’s hard to get people to donate to your project. And if nobody is donating to your project, it’s hard to become famous.

The way to break the cycle is to make something that people love, and then talk about it everywhere, until enough people hear about it, and then they’ll start donating.

But for some people, this is not possible. It might be possible for a musician to make music that people love, and then talk about it everywhere. But it’s not as easy for a software developer to do this.

This is why Marco’s announcement is so exciting. If he can successfully make money through crowdfunding, it will be a big step forward for this experiment.

### 4. New business models will come along

I think there will be new business models that come along that will make it easier to do this.

For example, Patreon is an example of a new business model that is making it easier to do crowdfunding. Patreon has made it much easier to create a community of people who believe in what you do and want to support it.

But I think there will be even more business models that come along that will make it even easier.

For example, maybe there will be a new business model where a group of people come together to support a project. Or maybe there will be a new business model where companies will donate money to projects they believe in. Or maybe there will be a new business model where people will donate their time instead of money.

We don’t know yet what these new business models will look like. But I think they’re coming.

### 5. It’s a good thing that this experiment is happening

There’s been a lot of criticism about crowdfunding, and about people who are trying to make money through it.

But I think it’s a good thing that this experiment is happening. We need to try new things, and see what works and what doesn’t.

If we don’t try new things, we’ll never get anywhere. We’ll just keep doing the same old thing, and nothing will ever change.

So I’m happy that people are trying crowdfunding, and seeing what works and what doesn’t. I think we’re going to learn a lot from this experiment, and we’re going to see some new and exciting things come out of it.

prompt: I almost never use my shell's job control (fg, bg, Ctrl+Z and so on). I just open another tab. Write a blog post explaining what job control is and the real situations where it's worth using.
response:
Job control in your shell is the feature where you can

- run a program in the background with `&` or `bg`

- pause a program with Ctrl-Z

- and bring a paused or backgrounded program back to the foreground with `fg`

I almost never use any of this. I usually just open a new tab in my terminal or a new window in tmux. But there are a few situations where job control really shines.

### what job control is

When you run a program in your shell, that program becomes the “current” program. So if you press Ctrl-C, it will kill the current program.

You can start a program in the background with `&`:

```
$ sleep 1000 &
```

You can then pause the program with Ctrl-Z and send it to the background with `bg`:

```
$ sleep 1000
^Z
$ bg
```

Or you can bring a background job back to the foreground with `fg`

```
$ fg
sleep 1000
```

Job control is a bit of a weird feature, and I’m not sure that it’s used that much. I mostly just open a new terminal window.

But there are a few situations where I use job control, and they’re really great!

### 1. pausing and resuming a program

Let’s say you’re running a program that’s going to take a long time, but you need to pause it for a while. So you press Ctrl-Z to pause it, and run something else. Then when you’re done, you can press `fg` to bring it back to the foreground and it will start running again.

Here’s the situation I run into most often: I’m running a program that’s going to take a long time, but I need to pause it for a while.

For example, maybe you’ve started an `rsync` to copy a bunch of files from a remote server, but you want to copy some files somewhere else first. You can do

```
$ rsync remote_server.com:/data /tmp/data
^Z
$ rsync other_remote_server.com:/data /tmp/data2
$ fg
```

and your first `rsync` will resume running.

This is so much easier than trying to figure out which files are already done and which files still need to be copied.

### 2. pausing a program that doesn’t support pausing

There are some programs that don’t have a way to pause and resume. So I use job control to pause and resume them instead.

For example, I can use job control to pause `ssh`

```
$ ssh server.com
$ ls
$ vim hello.py
^Z
$
```

It’s not obvious how to pause an ssh session without job control.

And I recently used job control to pause `rspec`!

```
$ rspec
$ vim test_spec.rb
^Z
$ rspec
```

It’s not obvious how to pause an rspec session without job control.

### 3. resuming a program

There are a couple of situations where I use job control to resume a program

- I accidentally hit Ctrl-Z and need to resume the program

- I accidentally run a program in the background with `&` and need to bring it back to the foreground

For example, I accidentally ran `vim` in the background

```
$ vim hello.py &
```

So I needed to use `fg` to bring it back to the foreground.

### 4. using Ctrl-Z and Ctrl-C

I don’t usually use job control, but I use Ctrl-Z and Ctrl-C!

Ctrl-Z pauses the current program (and sends it to the background). I use this when I accidentally run a program that I don’t want to run.

Ctrl-C sends an interrupt signal to the current program. I use this to kill the current program. I think this is the most common signal.

### 5. backgrounding a program with &

I don’t use `&` super often. I mostly just use it to start a program in the background.

For example

```
$ ssh remote_server.com &
```

I’ve also used `&` to run 2 programs at the same time. This is a little bit tricky though.

For example, here’s how to run 2 servers at the same time

```
$ cd server1 && python app.py &
$ cd server2 && python app.py
```

But to kill them both, you need to run `kill %1` and `kill %2` or `killall python`. So I don’t use this very often.

### why job control is important

Job control is one of those features that I don’t use every day, but when I do use it, it’s so helpful.

And it’s kind of fun to learn about – I didn’t know this until recently, but job control is implemented using Unix signals. This is a super important concept in Unix!

You can read more about signals in Chapter 2 of the Linux Programming Absolute Basics book.

prompt: I've written SQL for years but I couldn't tell you in what order the clauses of a SELECT query are logically evaluated, or why I can't filter on a window function in WHERE. Write a blog post explaining the order and what it lets you reason about.
response:
I’ve been writing SQL for many years, but I’ve never actually known what the correct order of evaluation was for a SQL query. I’ve just been writing queries that work and not working when I got them wrong.

But recently I wanted to understand more, so I asked the DuckDB documentation and learned about the order of evaluation for SQL queries!

### 1. FROM

`FROM` is always evaluated first, and determines what data you’re querying over. It can be a table or a query or anything else, and you can combine multiple data sources with a join (like `FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id`).

### 2. WHERE

`WHERE` filters out rows you don’t want.

You can refer to any columns in the FROM clause. But you can’t refer to any columns that will be created in future steps of the query.

For example, if you try to use a window function in WHERE, it won’t work, because the window function will be calculated later in the query.

```
SELECT
    window_function(...) as wf,
    ...
FROM ...
WHERE wf = 1 -- ERROR: "column wf does not exist"
```

### 3. Window functions

Window functions are like aggregations that you can apply to each row.

For example, `rank() OVER (ORDER BY x)` will rank each row based on its `x` value.

Or `SUM(y) OVER (PARTITION BY x)` will calculate the sum of `y` for each group of rows with the same `x` value.

### 4. GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` groups rows together based on some values.

For example, `GROUP BY x` will group rows together that have the same `x` value.

### 5. HAVING

`HAVING` is like `WHERE`, but for `GROUP BY` groups.

For example, `HAVING COUNT(*) > 10` will filter out groups with less than 10 rows.

### 6. SELECT

`SELECT` determines what columns to output. You can do any transformations or calculations here.

### 7. ORDER BY

`ORDER BY` orders rows in the output based on some values.

### 8. LIMIT

`LIMIT` limits the number of rows in the output.

### So that’s why I couldn’t use a window function in WHERE!

I’ve had this problem many times in my life – I want to use a window function in WHERE but I can’t.

For example, I want to get the top 3 rows for each group. I want to use `rank()` to rank the rows, then filter out everything that isn’t in the top 3.

But you can’t use a window function in `WHERE`, so I have to create a subquery instead, which is more complicated.

But now that I know the order of evaluation for SQL queries, I can reason about which queries will work and which won’t.

### You can use any column that was created in an earlier step

In general, you can use any column that was created in an earlier step of the query.

- in `WHERE`, you can only refer to columns in `FROM`

- in `HAVING`, you can refer to any column from `FROM`, `WHERE`, or window functions

- in `ORDER BY`, you can refer to any column from `FROM`, `WHERE`, window functions, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, or `SELECT`

So now I know why I couldn’t do certain things I wanted to do, and I can reason more about which things I can and can’t do.

### The order of evaluation for SQL is different than the order of the clauses

One thing I find surprising is that the order of evaluation is different than the order of the clauses.

The order of the clauses in a SQL query is:

1. `SELECT`

2. `FROM`

3. `WHERE`

4. `GROUP BY`

5. `HAVING`

6. `ORDER BY`

7. `LIMIT`

But the order of evaluation is:

1. `FROM`

2. `WHERE`

3. Window functions

4. `GROUP BY`

5. `HAVING`

6. `SELECT`

7. `ORDER BY`

8. `LIMIT`

### Different databases have different rules

I asked DuckDB for this list of rules, because I’ve been using DuckDB the most recently.

I think it’s mostly the same for all databases, but there are some subtle differences (for example, it seems like Snowflake and Postgres handle CTEs differently).

### I’m still not sure which SQL dialect is the best

One thing I still don’t know is which SQL dialect is the best to learn.

I’ve been using DuckDB the most recently, because I like it.

But I know that a lot of people prefer Postgres.

I know that BigQuery is super popular at big tech companies, but I’ve never used it.

And I hear that some people really like SQLite too.

I don’t know which one is best. I guess it depends on what you’re doing.

But I think it’s important to know at least one SQL dialect, because it will help you understand all of them.

prompt: How does the `locate` command actually work, and why is it so much faster than `find`? Poke at it on a real Linux machine, see if you can build a crude version yourself, and write up what you find in a short, playful blog post.

### What is `locate`?

Then I remembered, I should be using `locate`! I think `locate` works on Linux and FreeBSD.

### How does it work?

/usr/share/man/man1/hello.1.gz

/var/lib/locate.db
```

So if you do `locate locate.db`, you’ll find `/var/lib/locate.db` in the output! That’s the database.

The database is just a bunch of file paths. There’s not really any metadata in there. Here’s the start of my database:

```

### How is it updated?

`updatedb` updates the database. I think it’s run as a cron job.

It’s really fast – on my laptop it only takes about 3 seconds. I’m not sure why it’s so fast – `updatedb` has some C code in it which I think makes it faster.

### Can I make a basic version?

Here’s a basic version of `locate`:

```
def locate(needle):
    with open('/var/lib/locate.db') as f:
        for line in f:
            if needle in line:

```

```
import os

def updatedb():
    with open('/var/lib/locate.db', 'w') as f:
        for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in os.walk('/'):
            for filename in filenames:
                f.write(os.path.join(dirpath, filename) + '\n')
```

It’s not perfect, but it works!

I think `locate` on Ubuntu is just a bunch of shell scripts that call `updatedb` and `grep`. You can see the source here.

prompt: Write a blog post about what it really takes to start running a new, fairly immature piece of infrastructure software (a proxy, an orchestrator, that kind of thing) in production without causing serious outages. Draw on hands-on operations experience, and be honest about when this level of care isn't worth it.
response:
I’ve been working on running a new proxy service in production for about a month now. As with a lot of infrastructure software, there are a lot of things that could go wrong in ways that are not immediately obvious, and I want to write down some things I think about before starting to operate new infrastructure software.

I’ve had a lot of experience running infrastructure software in production, and in general, I think of it like this:

- it’s not hard to run infrastructure software that’s well understood and has been around for a while

- running newer infrastructure software is much harder

- it’s hard to know which category something falls into, so you should probably assume it’s harder than it is

There are a few reasons infrastructure software is harder to operate than application software:

- infrastructure software has to support a lot of different types of users, and users will use it in all kinds of different ways

- infrastructure software often has to be backwards compatible for a long time

- bugs in infrastructure software can be much harder to debug (especially if you have to debug them on a production system under load)

- infrastructure software has to be fast

- infrastructure software often has to be available 24/7

- infrastructure software has to work well when deployed at large scale

- infrastructure software is often not built by the same people who will use it, so there’s no “dogfooding”

- infrastructure software doesn’t necessarily have as much testing / QA done as application software

- if infrastructure software is down, it can affect a lot of services, so it’s much harder to do maintenance on it

- infrastructure software has to be fast and reliable, which means that it often has to be written in a lower-level language

There are also a lot of things you can do to make infrastructure software more reliable and easier to operate, but there are a lot of things you have to do to operate infrastructure software well, and there’s a lot of work you have to do to get it into a state where it’s “well understood and has been around for a while”.

Some examples of infrastructure software that’s well understood and has been around for a while:

- Linux

- PostgreSQL

- Kafka

Some examples of infrastructure software that are less well understood and haven’t been around as long:

- Kubernetes (though this might be on its way to becoming well understood)

- Envoy (though this might also be on its way to becoming well understood)

- some random new Kubernetes operator you found on GitHub

### How do you know which category something is in?

I think of it like this: if you’re using Kubernetes in production, you know a lot about how Kubernetes works, but if you’re just using it for a side project on the weekend, you probably don’t know as much.

You also have to think about the complexity of the software you’re using.

For example, if you’re running Linux in production, you probably know a lot about Linux. But running a Linux container is much easier than running Linux in general, because the container is only going to run a relatively simple application.

Similarly, you might be able to run Kubernetes in production for a relatively simple workload (like running a stateless service that you have multiple replicas of), but that’s going to be a lot easier than using Kubernetes to run a distributed database.

And if you’re using Envoy in production, you probably know a lot about how Envoy works, but if you’re just using Envoy as a sidecar to load balance traffic between 2 services, you probably don’t know as much.

### So how do you run newer infrastructure software?

Here are some of the things I think about when I’m trying to run newer infrastructure software in production:

#### 1. Make sure that the software is well understood

I don’t think I’d ever want to run a random Kubernetes operator I found on GitHub in a production environment. But if I really wanted to, I’d probably want to read through the source code to make sure that I understand what it does.

I also don’t think I’d want to run a random Envoy version that I just downloaded from GitHub in a production environment without at least having a basic understanding of what Envoy is and what it does.

#### 2. Start with a non-critical workload

I think this is probably the most important thing.

A good example of this is running a Kubernetes cluster in a test environment to do testing. I’m sure lots of companies have done this, and it’s a good way to start with Kubernetes. You can set up your own Kubernetes cluster on your laptop, or in a cloud provider, and then use that to run some tests. If the cluster goes down or there’s a bug in the cluster, it’s no big deal, you just restart it and try again.

But if you try to run Kubernetes in production on day one for a critical workload, that’s not going to work.

#### 3. Don’t run the latest version

I don’t think I’d ever want to run the latest version of any infrastructure software in a production environment. For example, I don’t think I’d ever want to run the latest version of Linux in a production environment. I’d probably want to run a long term support release of Linux (like Ubuntu LTS).

Similarly, I think I’d want to run a well-tested version of Envoy, not the latest version.

#### 4. Test it a lot

Obviously, you want to test infrastructure software, but it’s not always obvious how to test it.

For example, I think it’s relatively straightforward to test a proxy like Envoy. You can write integration tests that send traffic through the proxy and check that the traffic is handled correctly.

But I think testing a distributed system like Kubernetes is much harder.

#### 5. Have a rollback plan

I think this is probably the second most important thing.

If you want to deploy a new version of infrastructure software, you need to have a rollback plan. For example, if you’re running a Linux cluster, you probably want to have a backup of your Linux image so that you can roll back to it if something goes wrong.

#### 6. Don’t try to do too much at once

I think this is probably the third most important thing.

For example, I don’t think I’d want to try to deploy a new version of Linux to a large cluster of machines all at once. I’d probably want to do it in a canary release, so that I can see how it goes before I roll it out to the rest of the cluster.

This is obviously not unique to Linux, but I think it’s important to remember this when deploying any new infrastructure software.

#### 7. Don’t run infrastructure software without knowing how to debug it

Obviously, you want to know how to debug any software you’re running, but I think it’s especially important to know how to debug infrastructure software.

For example, I don’t think I’d want to run Kubernetes in production if I didn’t know how to debug Kubernetes. I’d probably want to know how to look at Kubernetes logs, how to check the status of the cluster, etc.

### What about application software?

I think that most of the things I’ve said here also apply to application software.

For example, I don’t think I’d want to run a new version of an application without testing it first. I also don’t think I’d want to deploy a new version of an application without having a rollback plan.

But I think that infrastructure software is harder to operate than application software, so you need to be more careful when running infrastructure software.

### What if you don’t have a lot of experience running infrastructure software?

I think that if you don’t have a lot of experience running infrastructure software, you should probably avoid running newer infrastructure software.

For example, if you don’t have a lot of experience running infrastructure software, I don’t think I’d want to try to run Kubernetes in production. I’d probably want to stick to using a managed Kubernetes service, or just run your applications on VMs.

Similarly, if you don’t have a lot of experience running infrastructure software, I don’t think I’d want to try to run a custom Envoy proxy. I’d probably want to just use a load balancer that’s built into my cloud provider.

### It’s okay to not run newer infrastructure software

I think it’s important to remember that it’s okay to not run newer infrastructure software.

For example, I don’t think that most companies need to use Kubernetes. I think that a lot of companies can get by with just using VMs and a load balancer.

Similarly, I don’t think that most companies need to use Envoy. I think that a lot of companies can get by with just using a load balancer that’s built into their cloud provider.

### Running newer infrastructure software is a lot of work

For example, I don’t think that a lot of people realize that running Kubernetes is a lot of work. I’ve talked to a lot of companies that are running Kubernetes in production, and they all seem to have a lot of experience running infrastructure software.

For example, I don’t think I’d want to run Kubernetes in production if I didn’t know what I was doing. I think it’s easy to make mistakes with Kubernetes that can be really hard to debug.

For example, I don’t think I’d want to run Kubernetes in production without having a rollback plan. I think it’s easy to make mistakes with Kubernetes that can be really hard to debug, so you need to be prepared for things to go wrong.

Similarly, I don’t think I’d want to run Envoy in production without having a rollback plan. I think it’s easy to make mistakes with Envoy that can be really hard to debug, so you need to be prepared for things to go wrong.

I think it’s important to have an intuition for why you have to make tradeoffs between consistency and availability. You should be able to understand this before you know what a quorum is, or even hear the term “CAP theorem”1. I think this is important because it means you can understand what tradeoffs you’re making when you choose a database, and also understand why the tradeoffs are what they are.

### A basic example

Imagine you have a database. You run one database server, and you have two database clients, called Alice and Bob.

Let’s say Alice makes a write request to the database, and then Bob makes a read request.

If the database is *consistent*, it means that Bob will see Alice’s data.

If the database is *available*, it means that it will return a response.

It’s easy for us to see how we can make the database both available and consistent. We just have to tell Bob “wait! You can’t read until you see Alice’s write.”

### A slightly harder example

Now let’s say that we have two database servers. Alice and Bob each talk to a different database server.

Let’s say that Alice makes a write request to server 1, and Bob makes a read request to server 2.

Now how do we get our database to be consistent and available?

One way we could do it is to make sure that all reads and writes have to go to both servers. So we’d have to ask Alice to write her data to server 1 and server 2, and then we’d have to ask Bob to read from both server 1 and server 2, and then Bob would get Alice’s data.

If we did that, then we could have consistency and availability.

### A harder example

OK, let’s say we have two database servers, and we want to be able to make reads and writes only go to one server. This is nice because we can split the load between the two servers.

Now suppose that the network is down. Server 1 can’t talk to server 2.

Suppose that Alice makes a write request to server 1, and Bob makes a read request to server 2.

Now it’s impossible to have both consistency and availability. We can either:

- Have consistency but not availability. We could do this by making Bob’s read request fail, so Bob doesn’t get a response.

- Have availability but not consistency. We could do this by making server 2 return its data, even though it doesn’t have Alice’s write request.

### A harder example!

Let’s look at a more realistic scenario. Let’s say we have two database servers.

Let’s say that the network is down, so server 1 can’t talk to server 2.

Let’s say that Alice makes a write request to server 1, and then Alice makes another write request to server 2.

Now we have a problem! If we want to make sure that we’re available, we’ll have to accept both Alice’s writes. But how do we keep the servers consistent?

### A harder example!!

Let’s look at a more realistic scenario. Let’s say we have two database servers.

### The CAP theorem

If you’ve ever heard of the CAP theorem, you probably know that it says that you have to make a choice between consistency and availability.

prompt: I was helping a newer programmer debug and realized I've never seen a good guide to the process of debugging itself. Write a blog post pulling together what debugging a program actually looks like, step by step, with practical advice.
response:
I was helping someone debug a program yesterday, and it was pretty cool to be able to explain the thought processes behind debugging – the way I’d debug a program, step by step.

I was reminded that there are a lot of people who are new to programming, and that I haven’t really seen a good guide to debugging. This post is an attempt at that – I tried to put it all in a single place, so that you could go back to it when you need a reminder of the steps.

### what is debugging?

Debugging is a way to figure out how a program works. If you’re not sure how a program is supposed to work, or what it’s doing wrong, debugging is a way to get more information about what the program is doing.

You start with some kind of evidence – maybe the program is printing an error message, or doing something wrong, or it’s really slow. You try to figure out how to get more evidence.

I often start by looking for patterns – is the error message always the same? Is the program crashing at the same place?

If you’re not sure what you’re looking for, you can start by getting a ton of information – like by running a program in GDB, or by adding lots of `print` statements.

### how to debug

Here’s how I usually debug a program:

1. figure out what the program is supposed to do, and what it’s doing wrong

2. try to understand the program better (by reading the code, getting a stack trace, or running a debugger)

3. add `print` statements or make small changes to the code to get more information

4. look for patterns

5. try to make a smaller test case

6. make a guess about what’s wrong

7. go back to step 2

This isn’t an exact recipe, but it’s a good general way to get started.

### figure out what the program is supposed to do

The very first step is to figure out what the program is supposed to do, and what it’s doing wrong.

For example, if a program is crashing, what was it supposed to do? And what exactly is it doing wrong?

You can often get more information from your users by just asking them. For example, if someone says “hey this program is crashing!” you can ask them “what are you doing when it crashes?”

Or if it’s your program, you can ask yourself “ok, I need to make this program do X, and it’s not doing that, and here’s what it’s doing instead”.

### understand the program better

Once you know what the program is supposed to do and how it’s going wrong, you need to understand how the program works.

If it’s your program, you might just know the answer to this. But if it’s a new program, or it’s a big program and you’re not sure how it works, you’ll need to dig into the program and get more information.

You can do this in a lot of different ways – reading the code, running a debugger, adding `print` statements, running the program with a different input, and so on.

If you’re running a debugger, you can look at the stack trace to see where the error happened, and which function called it.

If the error happens a lot, you can start by just looking at the stack trace to see where the error is coming from.

### add print statements or make small changes

Once you understand the program better, you can try to get more information. You can do this by adding `print` statements to the program, or by making a small change to the program.

For example, if a program crashes, you can add a `print` statement right before the crash to see what the state of the program is at that point.

Or you can try to fix the problem, and see if it makes the problem worse or better. (It’s usually a bad idea to make a big change at this point – if you do that, and it fixes the problem, you still won’t know what the problem was!)

### look for patterns

Once you’ve run the program a couple of times, you can try to look for patterns.

For example, maybe there’s a pattern in the error messages – like maybe the program is always crashing with an out-of-bounds error.

Or maybe it only happens when you run the program with a certain command line argument.

### make a smaller test case

Another thing that can help is to make a smaller test case. If you can’t figure out how to make a smaller test case, that’s OK – it’s not always possible.

For example, if a program is only crashing 1 time out of 10, and you don’t know why, it might be impossible to make a smaller test case.

### make a guess about what’s wrong

After you’ve gathered some information, you can try to make a guess about what the problem is.

It’s OK to make a guess that’s completely wrong – you’re just making a guess! If it’s wrong, you can always make another guess.

### use a debugger

If you’re trying to figure out how a program works, it’s often helpful to use a debugger. The basics of debugging in GDB are:

- run your program in GDB

- set a breakpoint

- run the program

- once it hits a breakpoint, you can step through the program one line at a time

- you can also print variables

If you’re using Python, you can use `pdb` instead of GDB (it works in a similar way).

Here’s a GDB example from a real program. I’m trying to figure out how to run this program in GDB.

Here’s what I did:

- run the program in GDB

- set a breakpoint in `main`

- run the program

- it hit the breakpoint

- I ran `print argv[1]` to see what the first command line argument is

- I ran `print argv[2]` to see what the second command line argument is

- I ran `continue` to continue running the program

### use strace

Another cool tool for debugging is `strace`, which lets you see what system calls your program is making.

Here’s an example of using `strace` on a random program:

```
$ strace ls
execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls"], [/* 26 vars */]) = 0
brk(0)                                  = 0x1a89000
mmap(NULL, 4096, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7fc340c54000
access("/etc/ld.so.nohwcap", F_OK)      = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
```

### debug a program by reading the code

You can also debug a program by just reading the code, and trying to figure out where the error is.

I usually do this first – I’ll read the code and make a guess about what’s wrong, and then I’ll try to run the program or read the code more to figure out if I’m right.

### debug by asking someone

Another way to debug a program is to ask someone. Sometimes it’s useful to just ask someone what the problem is, and they might know the answer.

### debug by turning the code into a different language

I’ve also been successful at debugging code by turning it into a different language. For example, I’ve turned some C++ code into Python, and then I was able to understand it better.

### debug by asking the computer to make changes

Sometimes I’ll ask the computer to make changes to my code, and I’ll look at those changes to see if they’re correct. If they’re not, I’ll try to figure out why they’re not.

This is kind of like making a guess – it’s a guess by the computer instead of me.

### make small changes to get more information

If you’re not sure what’s wrong, you can try to make a small change to the program to see if it makes the problem worse or better.

For example, maybe you want to see if the problem is caused by something specific. If so, you can try to turn it off, and see if the problem goes away.

Or you can try to do the opposite – turn something on, and see if it makes the problem go away.

This is kind of like running an experiment.

### use `printf` to print variables

A lot of the time when I’m debugging, I just use `printf` to print variables. It’s pretty simple and easy to do.

I usually just print out everything I’m not sure about, and then I look at the output to see if it’s correct.

Here’s an example – I was trying to figure out how to call this function, and I wasn’t sure what to pass in as the first argument. So I wrote a function called `printf` to print out the value of the first argument.

```
void printf(char *s, int c) {
  printf("%s %d\n", s, c);
}
```

Then I just looked at the output to see what the value was.

### don’t make big changes

I try not to make big changes to the code when I’m debugging.

If I make a big change, and it fixes the problem, I won’t know what the problem was, and that’s not useful.

So I usually make a small change, and see if it fixes the problem.

### use a version control system

I usually use `git` when I’m debugging, so that I can see what changes I’ve made to the code.

I usually just make a commit for every small change I make, so that I can look at my changes later.

### don’t panic

Debugging can be stressful, especially if you’re not used to it. It’s OK to take a break if you need to.

I usually stop debugging when I get stuck, and I’ll come back to it later.
