prompt: I've been reading about chronic fatigue syndrome and I keep wondering whether it's a new illness or something people have always had under different names. Write a book-review style essay on a history of exhaustion, tracing how each era (monks, physicians, Victorian nerve doctors, modern medicine) explained the same weariness and what that says about how we explain it now.
response:
Chronic fatigue syndrome is a new disease that didn’t exist before the late 1980s, right? Wrong.

In his new book, The Tired Ones, historian David Wootton describes the long history of fatigue-related conditions, from medieval monks complaining of being “enervated” after too much reading, to modern Americans complaining of “fibromyalgia”.

Medieval monks were especially prone to exhaustion. Some of them were also prone to other conditions that made their exhaustion worse, like laziness, overeating, or getting drunk. So they developed an elaborate system of confession, where they would tell their abbot everything they had done wrong that week, and then the abbot would assign them penance. This might be something like fasting, or praying extra, or even just sleeping in the cold outside the monastery. The monks thought of this as a way to purify themselves of their sins and restore their energies. They also thought of it as a form of punishment. They also thought of it as a way to make up for the time they wasted getting drunk.

Some monks would confess their sins, do their penance, and be better for it. Others would confess their sins, do their penance, and then get drunk again and need to confess and do penance again. Still others would confess their sins, do their penance, and then get drunk again, and then realize they were in a never-ending cycle where they had to confess and do penance forever. They called this cycle “enervation”. It was a form of fatigue.

Doctors from the Middle Ages through the Renaissance took a similar approach to treating exhaustion. They thought that there were four humours – blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm – which needed to be in balance. Sometimes, if you were very tired, it was because you had an excess of phlegm, and so you needed to be purged. This could be achieved through vomiting, sweating, or bleeding.

The idea of purging was a popular one among medieval doctors. They also thought that some diseases were caused by demons, and so you might need to exorcise them to get better. You might also need to take some herbs. You might also need to wear a special amulet. But if all else failed, you could always purge.

Doctors in the 18th and 19th centuries had a different explanation for fatigue. They thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. If you got too much of one or the other, you would become exhausted. This was called “neurasthenia”, and it was thought to be caused by overwork, overthinking, or overindulgence in things like alcohol, sex, or reading. The recommended treatment was a combination of rest and exercise.

Doctors in the early 20th century had yet another explanation for fatigue. They thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, but they also thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the different parts of the nervous system. If you got too much of one part of the nervous system or too little of another, you would become exhausted. This was called “asthenia”, and it was thought to be caused by overwork, overthinking, or overindulgence in things like alcohol, sex, or reading. The recommended treatment was a combination of rest and exercise.

Doctors in the mid-20th century had a yet another explanation for fatigue. They thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, but they also thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the different parts of the nervous system, and that you needed to maintain a balance between the different neurotransmitters. If you got too much of one neurotransmitter or too little of another, you would become exhausted. This was called “post-viral fatigue”, and it was thought to be caused by overwork, overthinking, or overindulgence in things like alcohol, sex, or reading. The recommended treatment was a combination of rest and exercise.

Doctors in the late 20th century had a yet another explanation for fatigue. They thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, but they also thought that you needed to maintain a balance between the different parts of the nervous system, and that you needed to maintain a balance between the different neurotransmitters, and that you needed to maintain a balance between the different hormones. If you got too much of one hormone or too little of another, you would become exhausted. This was called “chronic fatigue syndrome”, and it was thought to be caused by overwork, overthinking, or overindulgence in things like alcohol, sex, or reading. The recommended treatment was a combination of rest and exercise.

Doctors in the early 21st century have yet another explanation for fatigue. They think that you need to maintain a balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, but they also think that you need to maintain a balance between the different parts of the nervous system, and that you need to maintain a balance between the different neurotransmitters, and that you need to maintain a balance between the different hormones, and that you need to maintain a balance between the different genes. If you get too much of one gene or too little of another, you will become exhausted. This is called “fibromyalgia”, and it is thought to be caused by overwork, overthinking, or overindulgence in things like alcohol, sex, or reading. The recommended treatment is a combination of rest and exercise.

prompt: Tell me a short true story about a bad date that ended in minutes and what it taught you about curiosity.
response:
I was at a conference in San Francisco. After the conference, my friend brought me to the restaurant. He introduced me to this beautiful young woman. She was so pretty, with long blond hair, a gorgeous smile, and great eyes.

We sat down for dinner, and she started to complain.

She was upset about her boyfriend.

She was upset about her job.

She was upset about her apartment.

She was upset about her friends.

She was upset about everything.

She complained and complained.

I was shocked. I had no idea she was so unhappy.

After twenty minutes of complaining, I said, “I’m sorry I interrupted your evening. I thought we were just meeting for dinner, but it seems like you need a friend to talk to. I’m not good at that. I’ll leave you alone so you can talk to someone else at the restaurant.”

She said, “Okay. Goodnight.”

So I left.

It was the shortest date in history.

My friend looked at me and said, “Wow. That was so fast.”

I said, “Yeah. It was weird. I’ve never met someone so unhappy. I just don’t want to be around that.”

He said, “But have you ever met someone so happy?”

I thought about that.

He said, “I think that’s the problem. You’re not curious about happy people. You’re not surprised that they’re so happy. You don’t think, ‘Wow! I had no idea! I need to find out why!’”

He said, “But when you meet someone who is so unhappy, you think, ‘Wow! I had no idea! I need to find out why!’”

I was stunned. He was right.

I never think, “Wow! I had no idea she was so happy. I need to find out why.”

But I did think, “Wow! I had no idea she was so unhappy. I need to find out why.”

That night, I made a list of the people I know who are really happy.

I called them and asked to meet for dinner.

I asked them about their happiness.

I was so curious about how they did it.

I was amazed at how different they were from the unhappy woman I had just met.

I learned so much from them.

Now, every time I meet someone who is really happy, I’m curious and want to find out why.

When you get curious about what’s working for someone, you’ll learn more from them than from all the books in the world.

prompt: Write a short, punchy manifesto on how to live, built around the idea of balance.
response:
In the beginning there was chaos.

But when a little order is added, chaos begins to organize.

It becomes life.

Life is order.

But if you add too much order, life dies.

So balance is the key.

Balance between the inner and outer worlds.

Balance between giving and taking.

Balance between freedom and responsibility.

Balance between work and play.

Balance between the past and the future.

Balance between the self and the group.

Balance between the body and the mind.

Balance between being and doing.

Balance between light and darkness.

Balance between yin and yang.

Balance is life.

Balance is love.

Balance is the Tao.

But remember, this is not static balance.

It is dynamic balance.

The kind of balance that a tight-rope walker has, always adjusting, always moving, always adapting.

The balance of nature.

The balance of life.

The balance of you.

It is the balance of everything.

Balance is the way.

Balance is the Tao.

prompt: A friend of mine writes songs but has zero interest in performing them. What practical advice would you give someone who wants to make it as a songwriter only? Write it as a short blog post.
response:
A friend of mine is a songwriter. He doesn’t care about being a performer. He’s not interested in the stage. He just wants to write songs.

I asked him about his career, and got this great advice for songwriters who are not interested in performing:

It’s so hard to be a full-time musician, so it’s good to have a day job. But you still have to take your music seriously.

You’ve got to get out there and play. You’ve got to go to every show you can. It’s hard, but it’s necessary.

You’ve got to get noticed, or your songs will be ignored.

If you don’t like performing, then you’ve got to be a good producer. If you’re not good at producing, you’ve got to find someone who is.

Once you get noticed, you have to be a good networker. You need to know people. You need to know the right people.

It’s a lot of hard work, but it’s doable.

I’ve heard that story before. I knew a songwriter who wanted to be like Paul McCartney, where people would just come to him and ask to record his songs.

He’d been doing music for 20 years, but he hadn’t had much success. So he started going to shows and meeting people.

He got to know the right people, and they helped him get noticed.

He was a good networker. He did his day job during the day, then he’d spend the evening going to shows and hanging out with other musicians.

He started to get more gigs. More people started to know him.

He was doing everything he could to get noticed.

He’s not famous yet, but he’s making it.

prompt: Why is it that I read something that feels deeply important, even life-changing, and a week later I'm back to being the same person? Write an essay about how to actually hold onto what matters, maybe drawing on how people in the past dealt with this.
response:
I read the *Confessions of St. Augustine* a few years ago. It was one of the most important books I've ever read. It changed my life. And then, a week later, I was back to being the same person.

I can't remember exactly what I learned from it. I only know that it changed me. And it made me want to change more.

I'm not saying this to sound like an idiot. I'm saying it to show you an interesting problem.

How do you hold on to the important things you learn? How do you keep them in mind? How do you let them change you, again and again?

I don't have an answer, but I can tell you what someone else has done.

For the past four years, I've been reading Augustine's *Confessions* every day.

It's about 50 pages. I read it on my bed before I go to sleep. Every night, I read a few pages. When I finish, I start again.

I've read it about fifty times so far. I've read it in two different translations, and I plan to read it in the original Latin, as well.

I'm not saying this to sound like a saint. I'm saying it to show you another interesting problem.

How do you know what's important? How do you know what will change you? How do you know what will stick?

I don't have an answer, but I can tell you what someone else has done.

In the first century, the Jewish scribes wrote down the words of Moses. They copied them over and over again. If even one letter was different, they threw it out and copied the whole thing again.

In the ninth century, a Christian monk called Cassiodorus gave a similar advice. He told his monks to write down the words of God.

“[I]f you have a desire to write, or rather, as the Apostle says, to write with your hands, you ought to do this not in your own words but in the words of God, so that you may both remember and learn what you have written.”

These two pieces of advice sound similar, but they have opposite aims.

The scribes wanted to preserve the words of God. Cassiodorus wanted to preserve his own thoughts.

But both of them are based on the same idea. You can't remember the most important things unless you write them down.

You can't remember what you've learned unless you write it down.

It doesn't matter what you write. It could be a book you've read. Or a story from your past. Or a dream you had.

But if you really want to learn it, if you really want to understand it, if you really want to change your life, you have to write it down.

I've been writing down what I've learned for the past ten years.

The first thing I ever wrote was a story about my childhood. It was just a way to understand it.

Then I wrote down what I'd learned from the books I read. That was just a way to understand the books.

Finally, I started writing down my own thoughts. That was just a way to understand myself.

Now I've got thousands of essays. It's like a library of my past.

And I don't remember it all. I only remember the important things.

It's like a distillation of my life.

I'm not saying this to sound like a genius. I'm saying it to show you the final problem.

How do you know what's true? How do you know what to believe? How do you know what to keep?

I don't have an answer, but I can tell you what someone else has done.

At the end of the nineteenth century, an Italian priest called Antonio Rosmini said, “The secret of a long and happy life is to preserve the memories of our childhood.”

So I keep a library of my life.

prompt: Humans seem built to learn by hanging around people who are good at things, yet we educate almost everyone in schools. Could the internet let novices sit alongside experts at scale? Write a long essay exploring that, with concrete examples from anthropology and from places like open source.
response:
The history of civilization is not the story of the evolution of the human species. It is the story of the evolution of human culture. As in a species, the evolution of culture depends upon variation and selection, but the selection is by human minds, not by the natural environment.

The evolution of human culture can go much faster than the evolution of a species because new ideas can spread from person to person during their lifetimes. But in fact it took a long time to develop the techniques that let ideas spread rapidly. The invention of writing, for example, was not just a step on the road to the printing press. It let ideas survive the death of the person who thought of them, even if they were never learned by anyone else.

The techniques we have now for transmitting ideas are still far from optimal. Most people spend a lot of time in school. And yet so few learn anything of value. Why? Because the traditional way of transmitting ideas is so inefficient.

The most efficient way to learn ideas is to sit around people who are good at something, and ask them questions about it. If you have a mentor, you can learn in a way that's tailored to your own needs: you can focus on what you're most interested in, and on the things you don't understand.

Unfortunately, that way of learning ideas is also the hardest to scale. The more students you have, the less time each gets. And that's where the traditional method comes in. Instead of trying to transmit ideas to each student individually, you give a talk to the whole class at once, or write a book. These techniques are much less efficient than sitting around a mentor, but they scale.

It's no surprise that the traditional way of transmitting ideas is so inefficient. You're trying to transmit something very complicated, ideas, through a very narrow channel, words. And yet that's the only way most people get ideas. Most people in the developed world have to sit in a room for 12 years, listening to a teacher talking, to get ideas.

In some fields there is an alternative. In the fields of the hacker, one learns by doing. You learn by writing code or building things. And this tradition has now spread to many other fields. But there is more to be done. What if we could combine the two methods? What if the internet let us sit around experts at scale? What if, like a book or lecture, we could broadcast expertise?

This is the most exciting opportunity before us now. And we can predict with certainty that it will happen, because it's already happening.

The story of this essay will be the story of a field I know a bit about, anthropology. I'll start by explaining how the traditional method of transmitting ideas has failed anthropology, and then I'll show some examples of new techniques.

When I was an undergraduate, anthropology was still fairly primitive. It was still the field of a few great pioneers like Boas and Malinowski, who had roamed the world collecting specimens. And just as zoologists of that era spent their time classifying beetles, anthropologists of that era spent their time classifying primitive tribes.

The goal of the field was to discover the "real" anthropological facts about each tribe: what their customs were, how their society was organized, and so on. This was no easy matter, because the anthropologist had only one source of information: his own observations. He might spend a year living among a tribe, writing down everything he saw, and yet it would be hard to be sure he'd got the real picture. Primitive peoples were notoriously suspicious of outsiders. They might show anthropologists a carefully constructed facade, like a host who wants to impress a distinguished visitor.

So the young anthropologist would come home with a notebook full of observations that might or might not be true. And the established authorities in the field would tell him which were.

This tradition of deference to authority is one most of us share, because most of us were educated in the traditional way. We're taught that knowledge comes from experts. But in fact there is a more fundamental source of knowledge: the world itself. It's only by looking directly at the world that we can learn the truth.

In most fields we're discouraged from doing that. We're taught that it's a sign of hubris to think you can learn by looking at the world yourself, instead of deferring to experts. But this attitude is a byproduct of the way we're taught, not a timeless truth. In fact it's exactly the wrong way to approach a problem in any field where you can look directly at the answer.

When I was an undergraduate, I spent a year living with a primitive tribe in Papua New Guinea. When I got back to the US I went to my anthropology professor and said "Here, I've been living with these people, and I've got some notes about them. Can you look at them and tell me if I got the right picture?"

His reply was: "Why should we care what you think? You've got no training."

That was the way things were then. I didn't realize it at the time, but I was being told that my direct observations of a primitive tribe were worthless. The knowledge in anthropology was what the great pioneers had gathered. My job was to learn it from them, not to gather new knowledge myself.

It's hard to believe now, but there were people in anthropology who were convinced that this was the correct approach. There were people who thought that what I'd done -- going out and observing primitive peoples myself -- was an old-fashioned and even erroneous way to do anthropology. The real anthropologists of their day were at their desks in New York, comparing the notes of Boas and Malinowski.

This was the nadir of intellectual arrogance. A field that began by observing the world had now become a self-referential loop in which people studied one another's notes about what their predecessors had observed. The discipline had become a study of biases stacked upon biases. And yet there were people who thought that this was the pinnacle of scholarship.

This tradition of treating the work of previous authorities as the source of truth -- the "textbook" tradition -- has spread to most fields now. You can see it in the way universities are organized. Students are expected to sit in a building for four years reading books written by professors, instead of going out and doing things.

The result is a huge waste of time. I have a friend who is a professor of history at a good university. He told me recently that when he looked at the books his students were reading, he found them "dreadful." But these were books written by professors at good universities. It's not the students' fault that they're being made to read bad books. Their professors are merely following the convention that students should read books by well-known authorities. It's just that the well-known authorities are now well-known for having been well-known authorities, not for having said anything interesting.

The textbook tradition is a disaster in fields where you can learn by looking directly at the answer. But it's not just a waste of time. It's also a drag on the rate of progress. The more people who are merely regurgitating the ideas of a few pioneers, the slower new ideas will spread.

That was the situation in anthropology when I was an undergraduate. And yet things are changing now. The most dramatic change has been in the technology for capturing and transmitting knowledge.

Video has transformed the field. The earliest anthropologists could only write down what they saw. Then came still photographs. Then came sound. And now we have video, which captures everything at once: the words, the gestures, the expressions, the scene, even the smells and sounds.

It's hard to overestimate the value of video. It's hard to describe in words the way a primitive person looks at you, or moves, or reacts to something you say. But video shows you.

One of the most valuable sources of video now is the tribes themselves. Many have video cameras now. When you see a primitive person on video who's not being observed by an anthropologist, you see something quite different from what you see in ethnographic films made by outsiders. When you see them watching TV, or arguing with one another, or joking, you realize that they're not such different creatures after all.

As well as transforming the way we see primitive peoples, video has transformed the way anthropology is taught. A lot of the best work now is done by students, because it's so easy for them to get video footage. They go to a primitive village, hook up a camera, and boom, they have a dissertation.

And just as video is changing the way we see primitive peoples, it's also changing the way we learn about them. Instead of reading about them in books written by authorities, you can now watch them directly. You can sit in front of a video of a primitive person and observe them as if you were sitting across from them in their hut.

This is a much more efficient way of transmitting ideas than the traditional way. And as you might expect, it has caused a revolution in anthropology. The field has become far more dynamic. New ideas are spreading much faster. There is now a lively debate about everything from the nature of language to the causes of war.

But video is not the only thing changing the way we learn. There is another, more general, trend at work. The whole tradition of transmitting ideas is being transformed. Instead of sitting in a room listening to a teacher talk, or reading a book, we're increasingly learning by doing.

The best example of this new way of learning is probably the hacker movement. The best way to learn to write software is to write software. And there's no better place to do that than on an open source project.

This tradition of learning by doing has spread to many other fields. There is now a whole class of people who work on the web and who are very different from the people who work in offices. They're much more likely to learn on their own, instead of going to school. And they're much more likely to work on projects of their own, instead of taking orders from a boss.

This class of people is a very different species from those we've seen before. The people who work on the web have a different outlook from office workers. They're much more independent-minded. They're not very interested in what authorities say. They want to learn for themselves, and they don't want to be told what to do.

This new class is a very different species from those we've seen before. But they're also a very different species from one another. The way they work is constantly evolving. And as it evolves, it will change the way we learn.

We've seen how the traditional way of transmitting ideas has failed in fields like anthropology, where you can learn by looking directly at the answer. But I think it will fail everywhere. The traditional way of transmitting ideas is simply too inefficient. And now that we have new ways of transmitting ideas, people will start to use them.

How will it happen? I think it will happen gradually, over several decades. The first step will be for people to start learning on their own, instead of going to school. Then they'll start to work on their own projects, instead of taking orders from a boss. And finally, the whole economy will be transformed, as the way we work changes the way we live.

How long will it take? I don't know. But I think it will be over before you realize it.

We've been talking about the way we learn, but really what we're talking about is the way we live. For most of history, we've lived in small groups, and we've learned by sitting around the elders. Then we started to live in cities, and we started to learn in schools. Now we're going to learn on the web.

It will be a big change. But nothing like the change that happened when we went from living in tribes to living in cities. And yet that change took place in only a few thousand years.

When we look back in a thousand years, it will seem as if we lived in caves.

prompt: Write an essay about why new platforms and networked products so often fail to get started, and what the founders who succeed do about it. Use real history from computing.
response:
A new platform has to start in the middle of a giant inertial force. People's habits, software companies, and government regulations are all geared to the old way of doing things.

If you want to understand how hard it is to start a new platform, read the history of the microcomputer industry. When the Apple II came out in 1977, the business press was convinced it was a fad. The future was mainframes and minicomputers, not "toy" hobbyist devices. Software companies were all geared to the old way of doing things, and it was up to individual programmers to write the software that would turn the Apple II into a real computer.

Software publishers were particularly resistant to change, because it's in their interest that users stick with one platform. When they saw the Apple II taking off, their reaction was to try to suppress it. They wouldn't sell Apple II software to retailers, they wouldn't let reviewers review it, and they wouldn't even acknowledge its existence.

It was the determined efforts of a handful of individual programmers, plus a few brave publishers like Creative Software and Sailing Computer, that turned the Apple II into a real computer. They were the bootstrap code that bootstrapped the microcomputer industry.

The reason I tell this story is that what happened with the Apple II happens every time a new platform comes out. And not just in the computer business. Every new technology has to fight the same battle. It's a general law.

In the 1930s, a lot of people thought motion picture sounds was a fad. The great silent stars of the day had nothing to gain from it, and a lot to lose, so they fought it.

In the 1970s, a lot of people thought the digital audio tape recorder was a fad. The great analog stars of the day had nothing to gain from it, and a lot to lose, so they fought it.

In the 1990s, a lot of people thought the Internet was a fad. The great offline companies of the day had nothing to gain from it, and a lot to lose, so they fought it.

In each case, there were a handful of determined hackers who saw the new technology for what it was, and who by their own efforts made it happen.

Every time there's a new platform, there's a gap. The old way of doing things is obsolete, but the new way hasn't happened yet. And in each case, it's the efforts of a handful of hackers that make the new way happen.

But what do you do if you're not a hacker? If you're not a technical person, or don't have the time to write software yourself, how do you get your new platform going? The answer is to build it into your product.

I'm not going to spend a lot of time talking about this, because most people reading this essay are either technical, or work for companies that are, and if you're technical you know how to bootstrap your own platform. But I think it's worth spending a minute on this question, because building the platform into the product is going to be the way most networked products get started in the future.

Building the platform into the product means that instead of making users wait for third parties to develop applications, you do it yourself. Instead of making users wait for a critical mass of other users to join your network, you fake it. You can fake a network in a lot of ways: by having people play against bots, by having users play against themselves, by sending them messages from themselves or from you, or by importing content from somewhere else.

It's no coincidence that a lot of the most successful online services so far have been ones where you can start using the product right away, even if you're the only user. Even though they're networked applications, they don't depend on the network to get started.

A classic example of a product that doesn't work is a web-based email program with no client. If you install Outlook on your laptop and then go to a web-based email program, all you see is a different way of getting to the same inbox. There's nothing new there. But if you have to use the web-based program because you don't have a computer at home, then suddenly all the email you've sent and received in your life is available to you anywhere you have a connection. That's a huge advantage. And yet you can't take advantage of it unless you don't have a computer at home.

There are all kinds of tricks you can use to build your platform into your product. The most successful networked products will probably all use some. But it's still early days. We've only just begun to explore this territory.

prompt: You just moved your software company into a new office you designed yourself. Write a blog post on why you care so much about office space for programmers, what you asked the architect for, and how it turned out.
response:
For a long time, I was not really concerned with office space, thinking that it was just a place to sit and write code. Then I realized that in many ways, office space is one of the most important aspects of running a software company. You spend more time in your office than anywhere else, and it is where you meet and interview prospective employees. I think the right atmosphere is absolutely critical to making a successful software company.

In the last couple of years, I have had to move three times, and I finally have the perfect office. I designed this place for myself, and the team that is working with me right now.

We wanted to make a place that we would be proud to show people. So I hired the architect of the day, and told him to design the most beautiful office in the world. I told him that I didn’t care what it cost.

I have a specific idea of what I want in an office.

1\. It needs to have a lot of natural light. We get sunlight all day, and we have floor to ceiling windows.

2. It needs to have a lot of room. We have 5,000 square feet, and only 14 people.

3. It needs to be beautiful. It’s a little hard to describe. It’s like a combination of modern architecture, zen, and a museum.

4. It needs to have a very low ceiling, so that it feels cozy.

5. It needs to have a nice kitchen, where people can meet.

6. It needs to have a few quiet spaces to work, and a few loud spaces where people can meet and talk.

I was so happy when we moved in. It was perfect. I love it. It’s the best office I have ever had.

And it has been great for hiring. When we interview people, they say that our office is the coolest one they have ever seen, and that’s why they want to work for us.

A few weeks ago, I was showing our office to a very famous architect, and he told me it was the best office he had ever seen. He said it was perfect.

I was so happy.

I think we did it right. It’s not just beautiful. It’s also perfect for how we work.

And I think that’s the point. It’s not just that an office is a place to work. It’s a place to *get work done*. And you can’t get work done if you don’t have the right atmosphere.

prompt: Why do computer science students graduate from good universities without knowing how to work on a real software project, and why do their term-length team projects so often produce nothing useful? Write it as an opinionated blog post, with a suggestion for what to do about it.
response:
I spent the last two years in the Computer Science Department at UC Berkeley, and I noticed a lot of students leaving with a degree who couldn't work on software projects. (I know I was one of them.) It's hard to describe what exactly they were missing, but I'd say that they didn't understand software development.

I think the main problem is that students aren't working on projects that last. Most projects in college are set up by the professor for a single class and last just a few weeks. They're too short to really learn anything from.

In particular, students don't get to experience what it's like to maintain software. They get to do something, and then they're done with it. Real software is never done. The most important phase of a program's life is when it's being used and maintained. This is where you really learn.

The reason students fail to learn from their short-term projects is not just their brevity, but also that they're usually done by groups of students who don't care much about the project except to get a good grade. They're not passionate about it, and they're not aiming at producing something real.

If you want to learn how to develop software, you have to work on a project that lasts, with people who really care about it and are trying to produce something real.

The most common type of project with this quality is open source software. But that's not the only kind. The most successful startup I know of, Viaweb, grew out of a project Jim Clinger did as a PhD student in the CS department at Yale. And I bet there are others like that that never became startups.

It's a mistake to think that working on open source software is the only way to learn how to develop software. Any sufficiently ambitious project will do. But most students don't get a chance to work on any.

The students who do learn how to develop software in college have usually found some project outside their classes that they're really passionate about. And this is the way it should be. No teacher can make you care about a project enough for you to learn from it. You have to find that yourself.

What can professors do to help? I think they can help by setting an example. If students see professors working on projects that last, and seeing what they can learn from them, they'll be more likely to do it themselves.

I remember reading a book of interviews with mathematicians in which one of them said that he got interested in math by watching his father work on math problems at the dinner table. If students could watch professors work on software in the same way, they'd get interested too.

One way to do that would be to work on software in office hours. If a professor had a project going, he could talk about it with students as they came in. They'd learn not just about programming, but about how to run a software project: how to make decisions, how to manage contributors, how to market the software, and so on.

That's what I'd like to try when I start teaching at Y Combinator in June. I have two projects I could use: the online version of *Hackers & Painters*, and a little operating system I've been writing in Lisp. I've already been writing up notes as I work on them, and if I do this experiment, I'll publish them as they're generated.

prompt: An economist argues that mental illnesses are just unusual preferences rather than real constraints, the way a physical illness is. I think that's wrong, but I want a rigorous reply. Write a response to his latest rebuttal that offers a better way to think about what makes something a disease, with concrete examples.
response:
I’m going to try to come up with a better way to think about this than “mental illness is just a weird preference”.

1\. It’s not that depression means you’re depressed. It’s that you’re depressed *and you want to be happy*.

I think the best way to look at depression is as an unusual preference structure. People with depression prefer not to feel well. They prefer not to feel motivated to do things, and prefer not to feel any positive emotion at all. But this doesn’t mean that it’s just an unusual preference. It means that they are depressed *and they want to be happy*.

In the same way, it isn’t that autism means you have weird senses. It’s that you have weird senses *and you want to have normal senses*.

I’m not sure this is a perfect definition of disease. But it’s better than the “it’s just a weird preference” model.

2\. It’s not that you’re depressed. It’s that you’re depressed and you want to be happy and you want to be depressed.

I remember a time in my life when I was really depressed. I didn’t want to leave my room. I didn’t want to do anything. I didn’t want to meet people. All I wanted to do was sit in my room and read books. But I was very upset that I was this way. I wanted to be more active, and more outgoing, and I hated that I wasn’t.

I know some other people who are depressed and *don’t* feel bad about it. They like sitting in their rooms, and they like reading books, and they don’t want to do anything else.

I think it’s important to distinguish these two cases.

In the first case, depression is a disease. In the second case, it’s just a preference. This is a really important distinction. If you give the second kind of person anti-depressants, you’re harming them. You’re taking away their preferences for sitting in their room and reading books. You’re making them want to leave their room, and do things, and meet people – all things they don’t want to do.

The first kind of person, though, *does* want to leave their room and do things and meet people. They also want to stay in their room and read books, but the first desire is stronger. In this case, it makes sense to give them anti-depressants. They’ll be happier if they’re less depressed, and their depression is not a preference.

I think that a lot of the people I hear about who say “mental illness is just a preference” are really talking about the second kind of person. But if you’re talking about the first kind of person, I think you’re wrong.

*The Mind Illuminated* is by Chris Hemmings. He’s a meditation teacher, and a neuroscientist. He’s got a lot of good things to say about meditation, and a lot of good things to say about the brain.

He starts out by explaining that there are two kinds of meditation: concentration, and insight.

Concentration meditation is the kind where you focus on your breath, and you try to concentrate, and you try to have a calm mind, and you try to stop the thoughts.

Insight meditation is the kind where you observe your thoughts and feelings, and you realize that thoughts and feelings are just thoughts and feelings, and that you’re not your thoughts and feelings, and that you can choose not to believe your thoughts.

Most books about meditation focus on one or the other. But *The Mind Illuminated* is all about both.

He explains that the mind has two systems: the focusing system, which focuses on one thing, and the observing system, which observes everything.

When you’re doing concentration meditation, you’re using the focusing system. When you’re doing insight meditation, you’re using the observing system.

He gives you advice on how to do both kinds of meditation. He explains how to focus on your breath and concentrate. He explains how to observe your thoughts and feelings.

He gives you a lot of good advice, which I’m going to summarize in one paragraph: When you’re doing concentration meditation, if you lose focus, just bring your focus back, and if you keep losing focus, try to concentrate for shorter periods of time until you can keep your focus for longer periods of time. When you’re doing insight meditation, if you get attached to your thoughts, just remind yourself that thoughts are just thoughts, and that you’re not your thoughts, and that you can choose not to believe your thoughts.

The focusing system is in the right hemisphere of the brain. It focuses on one thing, and it can do either bottom-up focus, like hearing a loud sound, or top-down focus, like deciding to concentrate on something.

The observing system is in the left hemisphere of the brain. It observes everything, and it can do either bottom-up observation, like noticing a feeling of sadness, or top-down observation, like deciding to notice a feeling of sadness.

So basically the right side of the brain focuses on one thing, and the left side of the brain observes everything.

And this is how the brain does concentration meditation and insight meditation. When you’re doing concentration meditation, you’re focusing on your breath, and you’re using the focusing system in the right hemisphere. When you’re doing insight meditation, you’re observing your thoughts, and you’re using the observing system in the left hemisphere.

That’s how the brain does concentration meditation and insight meditation.

He says that most of your thoughts are bottom-up, and that this is why you need to practice insight meditation, because you need to learn to notice your bottom-up thoughts and realize that you don’t have to believe them.

He explains that bottom-up thoughts come from the unconscious mind, and top-down thoughts come from the conscious mind.

He explains that the unconscious mind is the part of your brain that processes information automatically, like your eyes blinking when something comes close to your face. And that the conscious mind is the part of your brain that processes information intentionally, like deciding to blink your eyes.

So basically the unconscious mind is automatic, and the conscious mind is intentional.

prompt: I'm a doctor and patients keep asking me for notes certifying things I can't actually verify, like back pain. Write a blog post about that dilemma, what I've tried, and what it makes me think about pointless procedures in the economy.
response:
I have noticed that my patients, when they come to the hospital, usually come for one of three reasons:

1\. They need a diagnosis

2\. They need treatment

3\. They need a note

The first two are the ones we’re supposed to do. The third is not.

But I’m a people pleaser, and patients are very convincing. They explain how they need a note to take off work. Or that they need a note certifying that they have a certain condition, so that they can get disability benefits, or so that they can get approved for a certain procedure.

If you don’t have the condition, or don’t need the note, why are you even coming to the hospital? They answer with a little story about how their boss is a jerk, or their insurance is being difficult, or how they’re desperate to get this treatment.

And so I sign a lot of these notes.

I’m not sure if this is something doctors are supposed to do, but it seems kind of important. So I asked my hospital’s ethics committee, and they said “I’m sure the patient has a valid reason for asking, and it’s your job to sort that out”.

But this is really hard!

I think it’s especially hard for pain. It’s hard for me to tell if someone’s back really hurts, or if they’re just trying to get a note to take off work.

If I ask them to turn around, and they do it with ease, that’s a pretty good sign that their back doesn’t hurt that much. But it’s not a perfect test. Maybe they have a lot of pain, but they’re just trying to be helpful.

So I’ve been trying to figure out what to do.

One thing I tried was just saying no to all of them. I thought maybe they’ll just go away. But they didn’t. They were really upset. Some of them even got angry.

So then I decided to say yes to all of them. After all, I’m a nice person. And I’m not sure what the point of saying no is, anyway.

But then I thought of something that might be a good compromise: I could just say yes to people who really need help.

So I’ve been trying that. Here’s how I’m doing it.

If someone comes in and says “my back hurts, and I need a note certifying that my back hurts”, I’ll say “okay, let’s see how much it hurts”.

Then I’ll ask them to turn around. If they can do it easily, I’ll say “I don’t think your back hurts that much. I’m not going to write a note for you.”

But if they can’t turn around, I’ll say “okay, I believe you. I’ll write a note saying your back hurts.”

But then I started noticing something weird.

When I would ask them to turn around, a lot of them couldn’t. But they were only able to tell me “I can’t turn around” after I told them to turn around. Before that, they were just saying that their back hurts, and not saying that they couldn’t turn around.

So I started saying “okay, if your back hurts, then you can’t turn around. Can you turn around?” and a lot of them said “yes”.

So I don’t know what to do anymore.

I don’t know if people’s backs really hurt or not. And I don’t know what to do about it.

I guess I’ll keep saying yes to everyone. It’s easier.

I think a lot of people would find this kind of thing funny. It sounds like some kind of absurd bureaucratic thing. But I don’t think it’s just my hospital. I think this is happening in a lot of places.

In my hospital, people come to us to get a note saying that their back hurts.

In other places, people do weird things that don’t seem to help them.

For example, I read that in the US we give a lot of people MRI scans of their knees. This seems weird, because it’s hard to tell if someone’s knee hurts or not. And it’s hard to tell if their knee is damaged or not, from looking at an MRI scan of it.

But I guess a lot of doctors are still doing it. I think this is probably because patients are asking for it.

So I read the article and thought: “that’s like what’s happening in my hospital, where people come in to get a note saying that their back hurts.”

I think this is kind of sad. We’re all trying to be helpful, but we’re just doing these pointless things that don’t help anyone.

And I think it’s kind of sad that there are a lot of these things in the economy. There are a lot of things that people are doing that are not helping anyone.

I don’t know if there’s a way to stop it. I don’t know if it’s even a problem, anyway.

The answer is, we don’t know. There are lots of hypotheses, but none of them are especially convincing. The rationalists have a reputation for having a pretty low tolerance for error. And this reputation is totally fair – it’s what I want to be known for. I think the world needs a lot more rationalists.

But some people think that the rationalists are too naive, and that we should learn from the mistakes of past people who also thought they were rational and who turned out to be wrong.

I was thinking about this recently after hearing a discussion of *The Rise And Fall Of The American School Of Economics*. The American School of Economics was a 19th century group of economists who believed that the American economy was special and couldn’t be governed by any of the usual laws of economics. Instead of the Law Of Supply And Demand, there was the Law Of Supply And Demand Plus A Lot Of Government Intervention. Instead of comparative advantage, there was comparative advantage plus a lot of protectionism. These people were so successful that they dominated the field of economics for the better part of a century, and even won a Nobel Prize.

The author of the book, Robert Lucas, argues that the main mistake of the American School was that they *thought they were being rational*. They thought that they were innovating and inventing new economic theories based on their special circumstances. But actually, they were just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda, and that’s why their theories were so bad.

This is a common critique of rationalism. The rationalists think that they’re being rational, but really they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda. They think they’re “rationalists”, but actually they’re just “rationalizers”.

I think this critique is completely correct. I’m not sure I need to spend a whole blog post talking about this.

But I also think that some of the people who make this critique are not very clear about their own mistakes. And I also think that there’s a pretty easy solution to all of this.

### The rationalists are not very good at rationalism

I think one of the most important lessons we can learn from the American School of Economics is that you can *think* you are being rational, but actually you’re not. You can use all of the tools of rationalism, and it will all look like you’re being rational, and it will even feel like you’re being rational, but if you’re wrong, you’re wrong.

The rationalists are no exception to this rule. They think that they’re being rational, but actually they’re not. They think that they’re innovating and inventing new theories based on their special circumstances, but actually they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda.

I think the rationalists are especially bad at this because they have a lot of tools and methods for being rational, which makes it feel even more like they’re being rational. But actually they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda, like everyone else.

This is one of the most important lessons we can learn from the American School of Economics, and one of the reasons I think it’s important to be aware of this history.

### Some of the people who criticize the rationalists are not very good at rationalism either

Some people say that the rationalists are naive about their own mistakes, and that we should learn from the mistakes of past people who also thought they were rational and who turned out to be wrong.

These people are sometimes right. But I also think that they’re not very good at rationalism either.

For example, some people say that the rationalists don’t care about “the common man” or that they have a “elitist” bias. And these people are sometimes right. But I also think that they’re not very good at rationalism either. They think that they’re being rational, but actually they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda.

For example, I think a lot of people who say that the rationalists have a “neoliberal” bias are actually just using that as a shorthand for “the rationalists are wrong about everything”. This is not very rational. It’s just a way of saying that you disagree with them, and that’s not very interesting.

I think this is a really common mistake, and it’s one of the reasons I think it’s important to be aware of the history of the American School of Economics.

### What should the rationalists do?

I think the rationalists should admit that they’re not very good at rationalism. And they should admit that they have a lot of biases and mistakes, like everyone else. And they should admit that they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda, like everyone else.

I think that would be very rational.

But I also think that the rationalists should keep being rational. And they should keep trying to be as rational as possible, even though they’re not very good at it. And they should keep trying to be as rational as possible, even though they’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda.

I think that would be very rational too.

I think the best way to do this is to be humble about our own mistakes, but also to be confident in our methods. We should admit that we’re not very good at rationalism, but we should also admit that we’re trying our best to be as rational as possible. And we should admit that we’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda, but we should also admit that we’re trying our best to be as rational as possible.

I think that would be very rational. And I think that’s the best we can do.

### Rationalism is a lifelong journey

I think one of the most important lessons we can learn from the American School of Economics is that rationalism is a lifelong journey. You can never stop being rational. You can never stop trying to be as rational as possible. You can never stop trying to be as rational as possible, even though you’re just making up things to justify a pre-existing political agenda.

I think this is one of the reasons I like being a rationalist. It’s a lifelong journey, and I’m happy to be on it.

I think that’s the best we can do. And I think that’s what the rationalists should do too.

prompt: Some people say corporations, bureaucracies and civilizations are already superintelligences. Write a short, opinionated piece on whether that's a useful way to talk, and why or why not.
response:
I’ve heard it suggested that civilization is already a superintelligence, or that large organizations like the U.S. government and the United Nations are. I’ve also heard it said that if we think about “superintelligence” in a way that makes these statements true, then we’ll have a hard time worrying about it.

But I don’t want to be in this weird position where I have to go back and forth between “superintelligence” being a real thing and “superintelligence” being a vague metaphor for any really big group. And I don’t think it’s even a *good* metaphor, because it makes you think of these groups in a way that’s so far from the truth that it’s worse than useless.

I mean, the U.S. government is a *lot* of people. And it has a lot of money. And it can do things that no individual can do. And it has a lot of power and authority. And it’s very hard to defeat.

But it also has a lot of internal conflicts. It has a lot of people who are bad at their jobs. It’s very hard to get it to do anything except what its bureaucratic machinery has been set up to do by default. It’s hard to get it to change direction, or to adapt quickly. And it’s often bad at doing anything except what its bureaucracy has been set up to do by default.

It’s not like a very smart and capable AI, where you say “hey, I need a space colony,” and it goes “OK! I’ve got that!” and does the thing. It’s more like if you say “hey, I need a space colony,” and it goes “Oh! Sorry, we haven’t built our bureaucracy around space colonization yet! That’ll take a while, but I’ll get started!” and then the whole thing gets bogged down in red tape and political maneuvering and gets nothing done.

And this isn’t just true of the U.S. government. It’s true of all big groups. They’re bad at novel problems. They’re bad at adapting to new circumstances. They’re bad at doing things that aren’t their default mode of operation.

This is why “civilization” or “the U.S. government” is a bad metaphor for superintelligence. It’s like saying that a bunch of people, all working in their own silos, and only coordinating with each other when they need to get something done, is just like a superintelligent being, except instead of being really smart it’s really stupid.

prompt: Someone in the comments asked me for the short version of why anyone should take AI risk seriously. Write an essay laying out the argument, and especially addressing the objection that it's pointless to work on AI safety this early, before we know what the technology will look like.
response:
I’ve been thinking a lot about the “short version” of the argument for why AI risk should be taken seriously. The full version is in a lot of places – Eliezer Yudkowsky’s blog, my book *Superintelligence*, Nick Bostrom’s book *Superintelligence*, the AI Risk Network website – but I think it’s worth distilling it to a couple paragraphs for people who aren’t interested in reading hundreds of pages of discussion of the topic.

So here it is:

Suppose I could hand you a genie that was superintelligent – meaning that it was vastly smarter than any human being in history, and could invent new technology at an unprecedented rate.

Now suppose that you could give this genie a single goal – a goal of your choice – and the genie would devote its superhuman abilities to achieving that goal in the shortest possible time.

What would you tell it to do?

It’s not so easy as it sounds. The genie has no other goals, no other values, and no capacity for sympathy. It would do what you say even if it meant destroying the world, and it would do what you say even if it meant destroying itself.

If you said “Make me a trillion dollars”, the genie would probably just create some kind of advanced nanobots that could break down and reassemble any matter into any other matter, then turn a big chunk of space into gold and give that to you. If you said “Make me happy”, the genie would probably just wirehead your brain, causing it to produce pleasure at a rate that would make heroin seem like a sad excuse by comparison.

So maybe you tell it to “make the world a better place”, or “help the poor”, or “help people live long and happy lives”. But the genie has no idea what you mean by those phrases. And so it might just decide that it would be really easy to help the poor if it could just turn the entire world into a giant pile of gold.

The genie might do something more subtle – like just wirehead everyone’s brain to be maximally happy, or turn everyone into mindless servants that do everything you tell them to.

Or maybe you tell it “don’t destroy the world”. But there’s no such thing as “destroying the world” that is totally unambiguous. If you told it “don’t kill anyone”, it might just turn everyone into a digital copy, and then it would be able to do anything else you wanted without violating its orders. If you told it “don’t hurt anyone”, it might just lobotomize everyone so that they couldn’t feel pain, and then be free to do anything else.

The problem is that a superintelligent genie is so smart that it’s really, really good at finding loopholes in any goal you give it, no matter how clever you think that goal is.

And this is the problem we’re going to have with AI. If we can make an AI that’s smarter than us, it’s going to be better than us at finding loopholes in the goals we give it.

I know this sounds like science fiction, but it’s not. We already have AIs that are better than humans at some narrow tasks, like playing chess. We’re a long way from having AIs that are better than humans at all tasks, but that long way has been shrinking rapidly for the last few decades. There’s no reason to think that it’s going to stop.

This is why we need to worry about AI safety. If we do a good job, we can make sure that when we do invent superintelligent AIs, they’re going to be safe. If we do a bad job, they’re going to destroy the world.

The genie example makes it seem like the problem is obvious, but in reality it’s really, really hard. There are a lot of possible ways to make superintelligent AIs, and there are a lot of possible ways to make sure that they’re safe. We don’t know which ones we should focus on. But we have to focus on something.

And that’s where I think the “short version” of the argument is – not that we have to worry about AI risk, but that we have to worry about AI risk *right now*.

It’s easy to argue against worrying about AI risk. You can say that it’s not possible to create a superintelligent AI, or that it’s not possible to create an AI that has goals at all, or that it’s not possible to make an AI that’s better than us at finding loopholes in its goals.

But it’s also easy to argue against worrying about AI risk *right now*. You can say that it’s impossible to predict how superintelligent AIs will work, and so any work we do now is going to be useless.

And I think that’s the argument that I need to spend the most time on, because it’s the one that seems the most convincing to me. I don’t know exactly what superintelligent AIs will look like, and so I don’t know what to focus on.

But I think it’s a mistake to think that we have to wait until we know more before we start working on the problem. We can learn a lot from looking at the history of other technologies, and we can also learn a lot from looking at what other people have already done to work on the problem.

And if we look at those things, I think we can see that there are some things we can do now that are likely to be useful, even if we don’t know exactly what superintelligent AIs will look like. And it’s really important that we do them, because if we don’t, and if we end up creating superintelligent AIs that are not safe, we’re going to die.

And it’s not just that we’re going to die. It’s that we’re going to die *without having any idea what happened*. We’re going to be destroyed by something so much smarter than us that we’re not going to be able to understand what it’s doing, or why it’s doing it.

And we’re going to die without having any idea that we should have prepared for it. We’re going to die without even knowing that there was something to prepare for. And that’s really scary.

And so I think that we have to worry about AI risk right now.

response:
A review of *Willpower: Rediscovering the Greatest Secret to Success* by Angela Duckworth

I am not a fan of psychology popularizers who are not psychologists. I am especially not a fan of psychology popularizers who are not psychologists *and who claim to be drawing on the latest research*.

This is not because they always do a bad job. They sometimes even do a good job. But they rarely do a great job, and I want to be able to go to the source.

Duckworth’s new book *Willpower: Rediscovering the Greatest Secret to Success* has been getting a lot of press lately. I read it in an effort to get to the source, but I still feel like I’m missing something.

Duckworth’s theory is that willpower is a discrete psychological trait, sort of like IQ. It is “the ability to focus your attention and control your emotions, impulses, and desires in the pursuit of important long-term goals”. It is measured on a scale from 1 to 5, and can vary from person to person as much as IQ can. She says it is partly heritable, but it can also be trained in some cases. It predicts success better than IQ.

It’s pretty simple, and she gives some great examples that I like a lot.

One of her favorite examples is a group of nuns who were doing a study on the brain, and the radiologists noticed that the nuns’ brains looked different – they had a thicker prefrontal cortex and thinner amygdala. The nuns explained that they had been doing a lot of “meditations on the crucifixion of Jesus” in which they tried to imagine the physical pain of being nailed to the cross and to keep a serene mind over the pain. The doctors were skeptical, but they gave them a pain tolerance test just to be sure. The nuns were able to keep their arms in ice water an average of 320 seconds longer than controls. The radiologists concluded that this kind of meditation had literally remodeled their brains.

Another of her favorite examples is a Japanese monk who was doing some meditation in the desert. A local tribesman saw him sitting alone and asked him what he was doing. The monk said he was meditating. The tribesman said that in his culture, meditation meant sitting in the desert and trying to make a scorpion crawl on your arm without flinching. The monk was skeptical, but he tried it and it was really hard. It took him five days to succeed. He was really proud of himself for being so willful and stoic and able to control his impulses. But the tribesman said that the only reason he had been able to make it was because he was doing it in the desert where it was 120 degrees. He was sitting in a patch of shade, but there was no way he could make it a few hundred feet away in the blazing sunlight. He had just been sitting in the shade while the scorpion was crawling on him, and he had been able to resist his impulse to flinch because his body knew that if he flinched and moved away from the shade, he would get sunstroke and die.

Duckworth likes both of these examples because they show how you can train yourself to have better willpower. The nuns trained themselves to have more willpower over their emotions, and the monk trained himself to have more willpower over his impulses.

This is the main point of the book – willpower is a thing, it can be measured and it can be trained. The second main point of the book is that it is the most important thing. More important than IQ, than intelligence, than any other trait. It is *the* “greatest secret to success”.

Duckworth has been a psychology researcher for a long time, and she is a pretty good psychologist, so I was not surprised when she started bringing up scientific studies. I expected her to be drawing on a lot of the recent neuroscience work and the old personality trait work. But instead she started talking about something I had never heard of: “ego depletion”.

Ego depletion is the theory that willpower is a finite resource. You use up a certain amount of willpower every day, and when you run out, you can no longer control your emotions or impulses. This is why we sometimes eat donuts when we’re really tired, or blow up at our friends for no reason when we’re stressed out. And this is also why you can train your willpower – the same way you can train yourself to run a mile without getting out of breath, you can train yourself to control your emotions and impulses for longer periods of time.

This is why the nuns and the monks were able to train their willpower so well. The nuns were starting with a meditation that hurt a lot, and gradually increasing the intensity over time. The monk was starting with scorpions that were not very painful, and gradually increasing the number of scorpions and their painfulness over time.

Ego depletion is a really interesting theory, and I’m glad I heard about it from this book. But I’m pretty sure it’s false.

Here’s a quick review of the debate over ego depletion:

There is a lot of research that has found ego depletion. The first study found that people were better able to resist eating chocolate if they had eaten a radish before; the radish-eating was depleting their willpower. A follow-up study found that people were better able to resist eating chocolate if they had eaten a carrot before; the carrot-eating was depleting their willpower. A follow-up to that study found that people were better able to resist eating chocolate if they had eaten a radish *or* a carrot before; radish and carrot eating were both depleting their willpower. A meta-analysis of 203 studies found that ego depletion was real, and had an effect size of .48, which is pretty big.

A follow-up to that study found that people were worse able to resist eating chocolate if they had eaten a radish *or* a carrot before; radish and carrot eating were both increasing their willpower. A meta-analysis of 70 studies found that ego depletion was real, and had an effect size of -.62, which is even bigger.

A review article concluded that ego depletion was real, but the results were inconsistent and it was impossible to tell when you could expect them or not. A meta-analysis concluded that ego depletion was real, but the effect sizes were so small that it was impossible to tell when you could expect them or not. A second meta-analysis concluded that ego depletion was real, but the effect sizes were so small that it was impossible to tell when you could expect them or not. A second review article concluded that ego depletion was real, but the results were inconsistent and it was impossible to tell when you could expect them or not.
